topics.title: Canvas reference
topics.summary:
A canvas is an immediate drawing surface. It has no meaningful children and
no CSS-painted content of its own; the host gives your callback a GPU context
or a recorder scoped to the element's box on every frame.

sections.title: Why it is special
sections.text:
ConcernHow Donkeh handles it
LayoutReplaced content with a default 300 × 150 box, or the width/height attributes. CSS positions and sizes the box like any other element.
ClippingThe host clips drawing to the canvas border box and establishes a canvas-local coordinate system before invoking the callback.
BatchingOnDraw records rectangles, ellipses, paths, text and images into the same indirect GPU batch as the rest of the UI.
Raw accessOnContext hands you Silk.NET's GL after the batch is submitted, for effects the recorder does not model.
BrowserNot wired yet. The DOM host mirrors a native canvas element, but the OpenGL/WebGL interop needed to run these callbacks has not been built.
Outside a browser, canvas drawing runs through Silk.NET against the same
OpenGL 3.3 context as the window on desktop, and the matching GLES context on
Android. That is why it is a real drawing primitive on those hosts rather than
a styled rectangle.

sections.title: Batched drawing
sections.text:
Prefer OnDraw. It records into the frame's indirect batch, so a
canvas does not force a viewport switch, a separate upload or one draw call
per shape.

sections.text:

Coordinates are canvas-local CSS pixels with the origin at the top-left of the
element's border box. The same CanvasContext instance is reused
between frames and is only valid inside the callback; storing it and drawing
later throws.
Balance your pushes
The host cleans up any clip, transform or opacity push you leave open, but
explicit Pop* calls keep sibling drawing deterministic.

sections.title: Raw OpenGL
sections.text:
OnContext receives a Silk.NET GL instance bound to the
window context. The host has already set the viewport and scissor to the canvas
bounds, so draw inside the element's box. These commands are immediate-mode and
paint after batched OnDraw content.
Use this sparingly. State changes made here are yours to restore, and raw
commands are not batched with the rest of the frame.

sections.title: Browser limitation
sections.text:
Canvas callbacks do not run in the browser
WebAssembly renders through the DOM host. There is no OpenGL-to-WebGL bridge
yet, so OnDraw and OnContext are not invoked on
net10.0-browser. Wiring a GL context through browser WebGL is a
large, complex piece of interop work, so it is not enabled rather than
emulated badly. The element exists in the DOM, but drawing from C# is a
desktop and Android feature.
For browser-only graphics today, use ordinary HTML, CSS, images and DOM
effects. If a canvas is optional, gate the drawing callback on
OperatingSystem.IsBrowser() or provide a CSS/DOM fallback so the
page still communicates the same information.

sections.title: Props and typed components
sections.text:
A component receives values from its parent through a props object.
Define a props class, then derive the component from
Component<TProps>. Inside the component, the current
payload is available as the Props property.
Defining custom props
Props are plain classes. Properties are usually init-only
with sensible defaults, so callers set only the values they need:
A props class does not have to derive from anything. Derive from
Props instead when you want its ready-made HTML attribute
surface, such as ClassName, Id or event
handlers, to be available on your props object.
Props is both a type and a property
In Component<TProps>, Props names the
current payload. When a local variable or parameter is also called
props, write this.Props to reach the payload.
The type keeps its full name Props.
Use the typed C<TComponent, TProps> overload so the
compiler checks the payload type. The untyped
C<TComponent>(object?) overload also works when the
payload is built dynamically.
Accepting children
When a component should wrap content supplied by its parent, derive its
props from PropsWithChildren. That class contains a single
Children property and nothing else, so components that only
want children do not have to inherit the whole HTML attribute surface.
Children is a Node?[]?. The parent builds the
nodes and the component decides where they appear. It is
null when the caller passes none, so use
Props.Children ?? []. F groups the nodes without
adding an element, which is what lets them sit directly inside an element
that also has its own children.
A component that needs nothing but children can use
Component<PropsWithChildren> directly:
If a component needs its own values and children, derive the
props class from PropsWithChildren and add the extra
properties, as PanelProps does above. Children are always
passed through the props object, not as extra arguments to C.

sections.title: CSS in the assembly
sections.text:
The [Stylesheet] attribute is metadata only. The CSS file must
also be an EmbeddedResource in the same assembly. The host
loads every declaration through Stylesheet.Load() and merges
them in declaration order after the built-in user-agent sheet.
Paths are project-relative

places; forward slashes are accepted by MSBuild and by the stylesheet
resolver. The CLI writes
src/Components/Name/Name.css.
Styles are ordinary CSS: class selectors, IDs, attribute selectors,
pseudo-classes, media queries, custom properties, keyframes and
transitions. The built-in inspector can edit the matched rules live.

sections.title: Hot reload
sections.text:
Hot reload is opt-in. Enable it once for the executable project:
The first command adds a reference that exists only in the Debug
configuration. The second runs the project through dotnet watch
and keeps it running. Supported C# edits, such as changing a
Render method body, are applied to the running process by .NET
Hot Reload. The development package watches source files, waits for the
patch to settle and then asks the window to re-render every mounted
component. Instance state survives when the hook order did not change.
Edits that require new types, signatures or base classes make
dotnet watch restart the app. Changing the hook order or a
hook's type is not detected automatically; press Ctrl+R to restart when
doing that.
Stylesheet edits take a different path. The desktop host watches the source
file behind every [Stylesheet] declaration and rebuilds the
entire cascade in place: user-agent rules, author sheets, style caches and
layout engines. CSS is marked Watch="false" for
dotnet watch, so a stylesheet save does not cause a build or
restart.
The build still embeds every stylesheet. At runtime the reloader prefers
the file on disk and falls back to the embedded copy when a file cannot be
found. Declared paths are resolved relative to the project that wrote
them, so both src/Components/Card/Card.css and
test-container/Styles/gallery.css are found from a test
container. Files are polled on the frame thread and read only after they
have been stable for one interval, which avoids loading a half-written
file.
Release builds do not reference the hot reload package, so neither its
assembly nor the file watcher is copied to the final application. The
feature is development-only by construction, not removed by a publish
step.
Set DONKEH_HOT_RELOAD=0, false or
off to disable it. Only declared stylesheets are watched;
external @import targets and embedded images are resolved by
the normal loader and cached for the session.

code.content:
donkeh enable-feature hot-reload
donkeh watch

sections.title: Provider rules
sections.text:
RuleBehaviour
NestingA provider inside another provider for the same context shadows the outer value.
DefaultsConsumers outside every provider receive Context<T>.DefaultValue.
Scope captureA component keeps the context scope it rendered under, so a later re-render does not silently change its view of the value.
UpdatesA provider is rebuilt when its parent renders. Put the state that controls the value above the provider.

Provider is not a component
There is no provider instance to hold state. State belongs in a component
above the provider, as in the App example.

One context per concern, such as theme, locale or a command service, keeps
re-renders predictable. A context value that changes on every keystroke
will re-render every consumer when its parent re-renders.

topics.title: CSS support
topics.summary:
Donkeh parses real stylesheets with a CSS engine rather than translating a
subset at build time. This page tracks the 168 property names the resolver
recognises, the selector features that participate in matching, and the
fastest way to get a CSS bug fixed.

sections.title: Selectors and at-rules
sections.text:
The engine supports type, class, id, universal and attribute selectors,
plus descendant, child, adjacent-sibling and general-sibling combinators.
Specificity, source order and cascade layers decide the winner.
FeatureStatus
Interaction and state pseudo-classes:hover, :focus, :active, :focus-visible, :checked, :disabled, :enabled, :required, :read-only and structural selectors.
Logical pseudo-classes:not(), :is(), :where() and :has() are recognised but flagged as unsupported by the matcher. The native host expands simple :is(a, b) selector lists before parsing, which keeps icon-font stylesheets working.
Pseudo-elements::before and ::after generate a box when their resolved content is a string. CSS hexadecimal string escapes such as \f0c9 are decoded. ::selection is matched and its background-color (or the colour part of background) styles the text highlight; color is stored on the computed style for hosts that paint selected glyphs themselves. Other pseudo-elements are ignored.
Conditional at-rules@media, @supports and @container gate matching. @layer participates in the cascade.
Animations@keyframes and @-webkit-keyframes are parsed; transitions and animations run through the style resolver.
ImportsThe data engine only records @import. The native host fetches HTTP, file and data URLs, inlines them and resolves relative URLs against the declaring stylesheet. The browser host lets the browser load them.

sections.title: Reporting a CSS bug
sections.text:
Use the CSS bug report form.
It asks for the property and revision, host, pipeline stage, minimal UI
tree, minimal CSS, expected and actual rendering, and reproduction steps.
That context is usually enough to turn a visual complaint into a failing
layout or paint test.
Make the reproduction small
One component, one stylesheet, no unrelated framework code. If the bug only
appears with other rules present, include the smallest set that still
triggers it. A screenshot plus a computed-style or layout dump is worth
more than a long description.
Reproduction skeleton
Replace the smallest relevant rule and attach the actual result. If the
problem needs a specific font, image, viewport or platform, say so in the
environment and notes fields.
Issue template fields
FieldWhat to include
Property or featureThe exact CSS name, selector, at-rule or function involved.
Support revisionThe short revision from this page, for example a68256d.
Host and stageDesktop, Android or browser, and whether the problem is parsing, matching, computed values, layout, paint or animation.
Minimal UI tree and CSSThe smallest component and stylesheet that still show the difference.
Expected and actualDescribe browser-equivalent behaviour and what Donkeh produced. Include measurements for layout bugs.
Screenshots or dumpsFrame capture, inspector style dump, or the layout tree. Drag images straight into the form.

topics.title: CSX syntax
topics.summary:
You love JSX in JavaScript and TypeScript? Here is the same experience in
.NET. CSX lets you build a full UI framework with markup-like components,
real CSS and a reconciled tree  -  and it is entirely optional, with a
plain-C# fallback for every example.

sections.title: What CSX is
sections.text:
A .cx file is a C# file with one addition: JSX-style elements such as
or
...
. The CSX toolchain transforms those elements into the ordinary _.H, _.C and _.F calls you would otherwise write by hand, then compiles the result as normal C#. The CSX project lives at github.com/barely-sentient/csx. Donkeh itself stays unchanged; CSX is a separate, optional layer on top.

sections.title: Setup guide
sections.text:
- Install the CSX command-line tool.
- Install the matching IDE plugin for VS Code or Rider.
- Add a csx.json to your project (the language server
creates one automatically).
- Write .cx files and run csx run.
The csx tool is published to NuGet as
CSX.CliTool. The IDE plugins are published as GitHub release
assets, so csx enable downloads the version that matches
the running CLI.

code.label: Terminal
code.content:
dotnet tool install --global CSX.CliTool --version 1.0.1

# Optional: install the IDE plugin
csx enable vscode
# or
csx enable rider

# Create a CSX project
donkeh new project MyApp --csx
cd MyApp
csx run

sections.title: Project configuration
sections.text:
csx.json sits in the project root and configures the
transformer. The defaults match Donkeh's helper class:
GeneratedFileOutput controls where the transformed C# is
written. Using src/generated keeps the output inside the
project so a plain dotnet run compiles it automatically.

code.content:
{
  "FrameworkHtmlClass": "_",
  "FrameworkHtmlClassMethod": "H",
  "FrameworkComponentMethod": "C",
  "FrameworkFragmentMethod": "F",
  "GeneratedFileOutput": "src/generated"
}

sections.title: How it works
sections.text:
- Parser: tokenises .cx files and
distinguishes JSX tags from C# generics.
- Transformer: rewrites JSX into configurable C#
method calls and writes a source map next to each generated file.
- Language server: transforms .cx files on
the fly and proxies requests to the C# language server, mapping
positions back through source maps. VS Code and Rider use it for
IntelliSense, diagnostics and navigation.
- Generated output: .generated.cs files
are ordinary C# and are compiled by the normal SDK glob.

invokes dotnet run on the project. csx build
does the same with dotnet build.

topics.title: Developing hooks
topics.summary:
Built-in hooks are protected members of Component. A custom
hook is therefore a reusable method on a component base class that calls
one or more built-in hooks in a fixed order.

sections.title: Create a hook base class
sections.text:
Name custom hooks with a Use prefix. Return the state and
actions the caller needs, and keep every built-in hook call unconditional.
A component derives from the base class and composes the hooks it needs:

code.label: HookedComponent.cs
HookedComponent.cs
TogglePanel.cs
TogglePanel.cs

sections.title: Compose existing hooks
sections.text:
Custom hooks can call any built-in hook, and can call other custom hooks.
The overall order must still be stable across renders.
Built-inUse inside a custom hook for
StateLocal values owned by the calling component.
StateWithUpdateUpdates that depend on the previous value.
ReducerNamed state transitions or grouped fields.
EffectSubscriptions, I/O and cleanup.
LayoutEffectCommit-time measurements and adjustments.
MemoDerived values that are expensive to build.
CallbackStable delegates passed to children.
UseRefMutable values that should not trigger renders.
UseContextReading a typed context inside a reusable hook.

sections.title: Typed component base classes
sections.text:
If components share both hooks and props, derive the base class from
Component<TProps>. The public props property remains
available to the derived component.

code.label: HookedComponent.cs

sections.title: Guidelines
sections.text:
- Keep the call order stable. Do not wrap a hook call in an if, loop, or conditional local function.
- Do not call hooks from constructors, lifecycle methods, or event handlers. Hooks belong in Render.
- Return actions, not setters, when possible. A custom hook can hide its state representation behind a small API.
- Keep hooks per component. Two component instances have independent hook slots, even if they use the same base class.
- Use effects for external work. Do not start timers, subscriptions, or blocking work directly in Render.
Hook slots are positional
The renderer maps the first hook call to slot 0, the second to slot 1, and
so on. Adding or removing a hook between renders changes the slot type and
throws. Keep the sequence stable for the lifetime of the component.

sections.title: Effects inside hooks
sections.text:
A custom hook can own a subscription and return its cleanup. The effect
dependencies are evaluated by the renderer; the hook itself does not need
to track them.
Keep side effects out of the render body itself. Return a value, or return
an action that the component can attach to an event, and let
Effect own the external lifetime.
Hooks can compose
A custom hook may call another custom hook. The same call-order rule
applies to the whole chain, so each call must happen on every render.

topics.title: Event reference
topics.summary:
Every host-dispatched event is represented by an event class. Simple
delegates remain available for compact handlers, while typed
On…Event properties and the matching element helpers receive
the full event object with its target, coordinates, value or key data.

sections.title: The event object
sections.text:
Event is the base class for every dispatched event. It carries
the data every handler can rely on, and concrete subclasses add payload
specific to the event family.
MemberMeaning
TypeThe normalised event name, for example click or pointerdown.
TargetThe deepest element involved in the interaction.
CurrentTargetThe element whose handler is running. It may be an ancestor when the event bubbles to the nearest handler.
DefaultPreventedSet when the handler calls PreventDefault().
PreventDefault()Marks the event as handled. Hosts with no built-in default action treat this as advisory.
StopPropagation()Records that the handler does not want the event to travel further. Donkeh already invokes only the nearest handler.
Event classExtendsAdds
Event - Type, target, current target and default handling.
MouseEventEventClientX, ClientY, LocalX, LocalY, Button, Modifiers.
ClickEvent, MouseDownEvent, MouseUpEvent, MouseOverEvent, MouseOutEventMouseEventEvent-specific classes for the mouse family.
PointerEventMouseEventThe same position data, typed separately so pointer fields can grow.
PointerDownEvent, PointerMoveEvent, PointerUpEventPointerEventConcrete pointer phases.

InputEvent, ChangeEventEventValue, the current or committed control text.
PasteEventEventText, the pasted text.

FocusEvent, BlurEventEventNo extra fields yet.

sections.title: Registering handlers
sections.text:
There are four equivalent entry points. Typed properties and element helpers
let the compiler infer the event class; On and Attr.On
accept any delegate shape.
Event names are normalised: onClick, onclick and
click all address the same event. Each element stores one
handler per event name, so registering the same name again replaces the
previous delegate rather than adding a second listener.

sections.title: Mouse and pointer events
sections.text:
Mouse handlers receive window coordinates in ClientX and
ClientY, and coordinates relative to the handling element in
LocalX and LocalY. The legacy
OnPointerDown, OnPointerMove and
OnPointerUp delegates receive the local pair directly.
A click is raised when a primary-button press and release land
on the same element without crossing the drag threshold. Disabled elements
do not raise it. mousedown is raised when the press starts;
mouseup is raised on release, including when the pointer moved
away. mouseover and mouseout track hover changes
for the whole ancestor chain.
Pointer events follow the pressed pointer. pointermove and
pointerup are delivered to the element that captured the
pointer, which keeps drags stable when the pointer leaves the element.
Touch input is translated into the same pointer events by the desktop and
Android hosts. The browser bridge raises pointerup for a
cancelled pointer. When a pointerdown handler captures the
pointer, the mouse press and release are not also dispatched for that
gesture, so choose one family per interaction.
Context menu
contextmenu is the one mouse-family event whose simple
signature is already an event object. Attach
OnContextMenu to a container to treat its children as one
menu area.

sections.title: Keyboard, focus and text events
sections.text:
keydown is delivered to the focused element. The simple
handler receives the formatted chord, while KeyDownEvent
exposes the key on its own and the modifier flags separately.
input fires while a text control changes and carries the
current text. change fires when the value is committed: on
Enter or blur for text controls, when a checkbox, radio, range or select
value is finalised. paste carries the pasted text. On the
desktop and Android hosts, a paste handler owns the edit and the host does
not also insert the text; the browser bridge prevents the native paste for
the same reason.
focus is delivered to the element that gained focus.
blur is delivered when focus moves away. The browser bridge
listens to focusin and focusout internally and
maps them to these two names, so application code uses one set of events on
every host.
Submit is a browser event
The browser host forwards native submit events. The desktop
and Android hosts do not perform native form submission, so call the same
function from a submit button's click handler or from
keydown when a text field receives Enter.

    onKeyDown={key =>
    {
        if (key.Key == "Escape")
        {
            ClearSearch();
        }
        else if (key.Modifiers == KeyModifiers.Control && key.Key == "K")
        {
            OpenCommandPalette();
        }
    }} />

sections.title: Scroll events
sections.text:
scroll reports the distance in CSS pixels that was actually
applied, positive when scrolling right or down. The event targets the
element under the pointer when a wheel scroll is applied and bubbles to the
nearest ancestor with a handler. On the desktop host, Ctrl+wheel is
forwarded with the raw wheel direction so an application can implement
zoom or brush size instead of scrolling the document.

code.label: Scroll payload
code.content:
<div className="scroller"
    onScroll={scroll =>
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"moved {scroll.DeltaX}px across and {scroll.DeltaY}px down");
    }} />

sections.title: Drag and drop
sections.text:
A drag starts on the nearest ancestor with
Draggable = true after the pointer moves past a small
threshold. Every event in one drag shares the same
DataTransfer. Write a payload in dragstart and
read it in drop.
EventWhen it fires
dragstartThe pointer moves past the drag threshold on a draggable source. Set Cancel to abandon the drag.
dragThe pointer moves during an active drag, on the source.
dragenterThe pointer first enters a potential drop target.
dragoverThe pointer moves within a potential drop target. Set Data.DropEffect to none to show refusal.
dragleaveThe pointer leaves a potential drop target.
dropThe pointer is released over a target that handles the drag.
dragendThe drag finishes, whether or not a drop was accepted.
DragEvent.Data is a mutable DataTransfer shared by
the whole interaction. Formats are arbitrary strings; use a reverse-DNS
media type for private data and text/plain for a readable
fallback. EffectAllowed and DropEffect are
descriptive on the native hosts.

sections.title: Media events
sections.text:
audio and video elements raise
play, pause, ended and
timeupdate. The media event classes expose the playback
position in seconds. OnAudioReady and
OnVideoReady are lifecycle callbacks, not DOM events: they run
once when the window-side player has been created.

sections.title: Host support
sections.text:
The virtual event surface is the same on every host. A few families are
produced by different platform mechanisms, and one is browser-only.
FamilyDesktop and AndroidBrowser
click, mousedown, mouseup, mouseover, mouseoutYes, from the native pointer pipeline.Yes, delegated from DOM mouse events.
pointerdown, pointermove, pointerupYes; touch is translated into pointer events.Yes; pointercancel is reported as pointerup.
scrollYes, from wheel and scrollbar drags.Yes, from the element's scroll offset delta.
contextmenuYes, from a right-button press.Yes, from the DOM context-menu event.
Drag familyYes, with dragstart from a draggable ancestor.Not forwarded by the bridge yet.
keydown, input, change, pasteYes, from the focused control.Yes, delegated from DOM events.
focus, blurYes, from the window focus model.Yes, mapped from focusin and focusout.

play, pause, ended, timeupdateYes, from the window media players.Yes, from native media elements.

sections.text:
These browser events have no Donkeh dispatcher. Registering a handler for
one is still legal, but no built-in host will raise it.
EventUse instead
mousemovepointermove
keyup, keypresskeydown
dblclickTrack click timing in a click handler.
wheelscroll; Ctrl+wheel is forwarded as a scroll with the raw direction.
touchstart, touchmove, touchendPointer and mouse events; touch is translated by the native hosts.
focusin, focusoutfocus and blur.
pointercancelpointerup on the browser host.

load, error, resizeHost lifecycle and media player callbacks.

sections.title: Dispatch and bubbling
sections.text:
Event dispatch walks from the hit element up through its ancestors and
invokes only the first matching handler. There is no capture phase and no
listener list, so an event never fires twice for one element. Registering a
handler for a container therefore acts as a delegating handler for its
children, and Target identifies which child was involved.
Handler exceptions are contained. A throwing application handler cannot
tear down the frame loop, which also means a mistake in a handler is silent
rather than fatal.

topics.title: Getting started
topics.summary:
The quickest route is a generated project. The framework supplies the
platform entry points, the root component, the stylesheet loading and the
host wiring. Your app starts at [AppRoot].

sections.title: Requirements
sections.text:
- .NET SDK 10 with the usual dotnet CLI.
- Desktop: Windows, Linux or macOS with OpenGL 3.3. The desktop host creates a GLFW window.
- Optional:
- Android: the .NET Android workload and an Android SDK. The generated APK is standalone.
- Browser: a .NET 10 browser build. No extra workload is needed for the Blazor-based WASM host.

dotnet tool install --global Donkeh.CliTool

# or run from a checkout
dotnet run --project Donkeh/CliTool/Source/Donkeh.CliTool.csproj -- --help

Run one of these from any directory. The CLI uses the published NuGet
packages, so no framework checkout is required.
The project defaults to desktop. The generated Program.cs
contains a single attributed root component, so there is no Main

For a reusable component library, generate a framework-shaped project
instead. It creates a packable library under src/ and a console

The test container references the library directly.

sections.title: The app root
sections.text:
[AppRoot] marks the component the framework should mount. Its
named properties replace the old IDonkehApp.Settings object.
Attributes are constants
C# attributes cannot take object initializers such as
new WindowSettings { ... }. Use the attribute's named
properties, for example Width = 1180 and
Frameless = true.
The framework discovers the attribute in the entry assembly, creates the
root component, loads every [Stylesheet] declaration, and
starts the matching host. Desktop and browser builds compile a generated
Main; Android uses the framework activity.

sections.text:
Desktop is enabled by default. Add Android or browser support from the

sections.title: Behaviour
sections.text:
- Granted results are cached for the session.
- Denied results are not cached, so the app can retry after the user changes a setting.

- Unsupported capabilities return false instead of throwing.
- Cancellation is best-effort; a platform prompt may still be visible after the task completes.

sections.title: Behaviour by element
sections.text:
ElementNotes
imgReplaced content with intrinsic sizing, source resolution, object-fit and a shared texture cache. See Image.
videoDesktop and Android use a LibVLC player whose frames become textures. See Video reference.
canvasDesktop uses batched Silk.NET drawing or raw OpenGL; browser drawing is not wired yet. See Canvas reference.
audioDesktop and Android use the window-side audio player and paint transport controls. It has no visual box when controls is absent.
inputText-like types are editable with click-to-place caret, arrow and word navigation, selection, scrolling to the caret and caret-color/::selection support. Checkbox, radio, range, colour and file inputs are host-painted and interactive. Other types still render as controls.
select, optionThe selected option and a dropdown chevron are painted by the host. Arrow keys, Home/End, Enter/Space and type-ahead navigate the option list. Option elements are hidden in the user-agent sheet.
textareaEditable multi-line text with click-to-place caret, Up/Down line movement, line-aware Home/End, selection, internal scrolling, caret and placeholder support.
table familyTable layout, collapse and spacing are supported. Use normal table structure; anonymous table boxes are not synthesised for arbitrary children.
picture, sourceParsed as elements, but responsive source selection is not implemented. img uses its own src.
webviewDesktop hosts a CEF offscreen browser whose frames become textures, so the element joins normal paint order, clipping and transforms. Use WebViewProps for navigation and script. See WebView reference.
iframe, object, embedRender a stable 300 × 150 placeholder box. They do not load or embed external documents.
script, style, link, metaHidden by the user-agent sheet. Scripts are never executed and link stylesheets are never fetched; load CSS through [Stylesheet].
Browser host
On WebAssembly the tree is mirrored to real DOM elements, so native browser
behaviour applies. Desktop and Android use the CSS engine, layout and paint
pipeline instead. Elements with host-specific behaviour are called out
above.

sections.title: Fonts and WOFF
sections.text:
The native host discovers installed system fonts by family and falls back by
codepoint. A custom host can add a font without installing it system-wide:
TTF, OTF, WOFF and WOFF2 files are accepted. WOFF containers are expanded to
sfnt before the normal metrics, glyph atlas and fallback pipeline runs.
RegisterFont wins over system discovery for that family; the
browser host delegates font loading to the browser instead.
The native host also resolves external author stylesheets. Absolute or
relative @import URLs are fetched and inlined, and each
@font-face block downloads its first supported font source and
registers the family automatically. Relative URLs resolve against the
stylesheet that declared them. Failures leave the original rule in place and
keep the fallback font chain.

topics.title: Image
topics.summary:
img is not a normal box. It is replaced content: layout must
know the image's intrinsic size before it can place anything, and paint must
upload, cache and fit the decoded bitmap. Donkeh treats it as a first-class
primitive rather than an empty element with a background.

sections.title: Why it is special
sections.text:
Pipeline stageWhat the image primitive does
Source resolutionResolves a file path, a data: URI or an embedded asset declared with [Image]. A plain path probes disk first, then packed assets; the packed:, embedded: and asset: prefixes force the embedded lookup.
Intrinsic sizingReads the encoded header, or rasterises an SVG, to get pixel dimensions. Layout uses those dimensions to preserve aspect ratio before CSS constraints apply.
Decoding and uploadDecodes RGBA pixels and uploads one OpenGL texture per source. Encoded bytes, decoded dimensions and textures are cached separately.
PaintingDraws the bitmap through the same instanced renderer as shapes and text, applying object-fit and object-position.
CSS backgroundsbackground-image: url(...) shares the same encoded-byte and texture cache, so an image used both as a layer and as img is decoded once.
Decoding on the layout thread would stall every frame, and letting an
img collapse to zero height would break flex and grid layouts.
That is why the host owns the cache and reports intrinsic dimensions back to
layout.

sections.title: Declare an embedded image
sections.text:
Add the file as an EmbeddedResource, then declare it with
[Image]. The attribute is metadata only; the file still has to
be embedded in the same assembly.
Path matching
A declaration may be matched by full path, a suffix or its bare file name.
Case is ignored, and folder-aware matching prevents
Other/logo.png from resolving to Assets/logo.png.
When two declarations match, the result is treated as unavailable instead of
picking one arbitrarily.

code.content:
<ItemGroup>
  <EmbeddedResource Include="Assets/logo.png" />
</ItemGroup>

Program.cs

sections.text:
SourceExampleNotes
Relative or absolute fileAssets/logo.pngProbed on disk first. Relative paths resolve against the process working directory at first use.
Embedded assetpacked:Assets/logo.pngUses the [Image] declaration and manifest resource in a loaded assembly.
Data URIdata:image/png;base64,...Decoded directly, with no disk access.
SVGAssets/icon.svgRasterised on first use, whether it comes from disk, a data URI or an embedded resource.

sections.title: Sizing and fitting
sections.text:
The intrinsic size comes from the decoded pixels, not CSS pixels. If the
header cannot be read, the width and height
attributes are used. The user-agent sheet gives images
max-width: 100%, so a large image shrinks with its container
while preserving aspect ratio.
object-fit accepts fill, contain,
cover, none and scale-down.
cover crops by shrinking the UV rectangle rather than clipping
the quad; contain and scale-down centre the image
in the box.

sections.title: Cache behaviour
sections.text:
BehaviourDetail
No evictionEvery successfully used source stays in memory until the window is disposed.
No file watchingReplacing a file on disk does not refresh the image. Restart the window, or use a new source string.
Failures are cachedA missing or corrupt source resolves to a zero texture and is not retried every frame.
Frame-thread uploadTextures are created and deleted on the render thread. Intrinsic-size queries can happen earlier.

sections.title: Browser host
sections.text:
On WebAssembly the tree is mirrored to a native img, and the
browser owns loading, decoding and layout. Use a URL or data:
URI there. The packed: and embedded: source forms
are for the desktop and Android GL hosts, which implement the packed-asset
resolver.
Need the bytes?
Use Image.Load("Assets/logo.png") or
Image.TryGetBytes(...) when you need the encoded file for an
upload, a custom cache or a non-img path. The element pipeline
uses the same declarations internally.

topics.title: Android
topics.summary:
Donkeh.Windowing.Android is deliberately small. It is the
framework-owned Android activity that boots the portable windowing stack on
an external GLES surface, applies mobile defaults, translates display density
into CSS pixels, and installs the Android runtime-permission provider. App
code still declares only an [AppRoot].

sections.title: What the package hides
sections.text:
The application project targets net10.0-android and references
this package, but never writes an activity. The host hides four things that
would otherwise leak into every app:
ConcernHandled by
Launcher activity and manifest entryDonkehActivity is the MainLauncher, exported, with a fullscreen no-action-bar theme.
GLES context and surfaceCreates a Silk.NET view with OpenGL ES 3.0, depth 24, stencil 8, no MSAA, VSync and a 60 Hz cap.
Density and lifecycleReads display density, converts the external surface into a CSS-pixel viewport and keeps the activity across configuration changes.
Runtime permissionsInstalls an IPermissionService that requests from the activity and completes from OnRequestPermissionsResult.

sections.title: The activity
sections.text:
DonkehActivity derives from Silk.NET's SDL-backed
SilkActivity. Its attributes declare a fullscreen Material
no-action-bar theme and a configuration-change set that includes orientation,
keyboard, UI mode, density, screen layout and smallest screen size. Because
the activity handles those changes itself, rotation does not recreate it: the
same DonkehWindow keeps running and CSS reflows against the new
surface size.
The SDL binding seam
SilkActivity is abstract, so .NET Android does not emit a static
JNI registration block for it, and the delegate getters that register
n_loadLibraries, n_setOrientationBis and
n_onDestroy are private on the binding base. The host
re-exposes those handlers for this concrete activity through
GetBaseHandler, which reflects the private static getter once.
DynamicDependency attributes keep the binding members rooted for
trimming.
Reflection is confined to the binding seam
This is one of the few places where the host reaches into private framework
members. The dependency is deliberate: it keeps the app-facing activity
concrete without duplicating SDL's JNI bootstrap, and a Silk.NET binding
upgrade that renames a handler fails loudly with
MissingMethodException.

code.label: Activity declaration
code.content:
[Activity(
    Label = "Donkeh",
    MainLauncher = true,
    Exported = true,
    Theme = "@android:style/Theme.Material.NoActionBar.Fullscreen",
    ConfigurationChanges = SilkActivity.ConfigChangesFlags
        | ConfigChanges.UiMode
        | ConfigChanges.Density
        | ConfigChanges.ScreenLayout
        | ConfigChanges.SmallestScreenSize)]
public class DonkehActivity : SilkActivity

sections.title: Starting the app
sections.text:
OnRun is the Android equivalent of the desktop entry point:
- Discover the [AppRoot] definition.
- Read Resources.DisplayMetrics.Density.
- Create AndroidPermissionService and install it through Host.UsePermissions.
- Create a GLES 3.0 view with a 24-bit depth buffer, 8-bit stencil, no MSAA, VSync and a 60 FPS cap.
- Clone the app settings and override everything the activity owns: size, chrome, VSync, frame cap, samples, resizability, devtools and DPI.
- Create DonkehWindow, run the view with the app root and merged styles, and let the shared window loop do the rest.
An app’s requested window width, height, frame style, MSAA, drag-resize and
devtools settings are therefore visual suggestions on Android, not contracts.
The surface, frame pacing and chrome belong to the activity.

code.label: Mobile settings
Mobile settings
code.content:
var settings = app.Settings with
{
    Width = 0,                    // the activity owns the surface
    Height = 0,
    VSync = true,
    TargetFramesPerSecond = 60,
    Samples = 0,                  // no MSAA on the mobile path
    Resizable = false,
    Frameless = false,
    EnableDevTools = false,
    EnableTouchScrolling = true, // swipe pans the nearest scroll container
    DpiScale = density
};

sections.title: Density and CSS pixels
sections.text:
Android reports a surface in physical pixels and a density scalar, not a
desktop-style logical window. The host passes density as
WindowSettings.DpiScale, so the window divides view and pointer
coordinates by it before layout and hit testing. CSS pixels stay independent
of the panel resolution.
Some SDL builds already expose a logical window size and a larger drawable.
In that case applying density again would shrink the UI, so the
Loaded handler checks the ratio and resets DpiScale
to zero when the framebuffer is already larger than the logical size. The
same handler prints density, DPI, size, framebuffer and GL version for
diagnosis.

sections.title: Touch scrolling
sections.text:
SDL synthesizes mouse events from a single finger, which keeps taps,
focus and app-owned pointer handlers working. The missing piece is
panning, so the host enables EnableTouchScrolling: a drag
over scrollable content waits for an eight-pixel slop threshold, locks
to the gesture’s dominant axis and scrolls the nearest container that
can move on that axis. Panning bypasses smooth-scroll easing so the
content tracks the finger. A press that never crosses the threshold is
replayed as a normal click.
Gestures that begin on a scrollbar, text control, range slider, button,
link, media element or an element with a pointerdown
handler keep their existing behaviour. Scrollbar tracks gain a twelve-pixel
inward hit margin on touch hosts, and touching beside the thumb starts a
drag instead of jumping the track.
Long press
A touch press held still for 500 ms becomes a contextmenu
event, so Android gets the same menus as a desktop right-click. Drifting
more than 10 px, starting a drag or starting a scroll pan cancels the
candidate. Once it fires, the click that would normally follow the
release is suppressed, so the menu does not also activate the item under
the finger.

sections.title: Runtime permissions
sections.text:
AndroidPermissionService translates Donkeh’s portable
HostPermission values into Android manifest permissions:
Donkeh permissionAndroid permission(s)
CameraCAMERA
MicrophoneRECORD_AUDIO
LocationACCESS_FINE_LOCATION, ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION
NotificationsPOST_NOTIFICATIONS on API 33+; pre-33 resolves true
PhotosREAD_MEDIA_IMAGES on API 33+, otherwise READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE
StorageREAD_MEDIA_IMAGES on API 33+, otherwise read/write external storage
Contacts / CalendarREAD_CONTACTS / READ_CALENDAR
BluetoothBLUETOOTH_CONNECT on API 31+, otherwise legacy BLUETOOTH
MotionACTIVITY_RECOGNITION on API 29+, otherwise unsupported
ClipboardResolves immediately; no runtime prompt
The provider first checks CheckSelfPermission for every required
name and returns immediately when all are granted. Otherwise it allocates a
request code, stores a pending completion in a dictionary, registers
cancellation, and posts RequestPermissions to the UI thread. The
activity forwards OnRequestPermissionsResult back to the
provider, which completes the task and removes the entry.
Any-of versus all-of
For a permission that maps to multiple Android names, the current result
handler completes true when any requested name is granted. Location and
pre-33 storage are the practical cases. Treat the portable boolean as “the
platform granted enough to proceed”, not as proof that every manifest entry
was accepted.
OnDestroy calls CancelAll, so every pending prompt
resolves false when the activity closes. The app must still declare the
matching uses-permission entries; the framework’s Android
permission targets can emit them from the central
DonkehAndroidPermissions list, and a hand-written manifest can
add more.
INTERNET is added automatically when an app stylesheet
references an external asset. The native host resolves remote
@import rules, their @font-face sources and
url(...) backgrounds at start-up; the build scans the app’s
CSS for http:// or https:// and emits the
permission. This matters for release builds because only debuggable APKs
receive INTERNET implicitly from the Android SDK. Set
DonkehAndroidInternet to true or
false to override detection.

sections.title: Android versus desktop
sections.text:
AreaAndroid behaviour
SurfaceActivity-owned GLES view; the app does not create a native desktop window.
Frame pacingVSync and a 60 FPS cap, regardless of desktop settings.
Chrome and resizeNo native title bar, frameless resize handles or window dragging.
MSAADisabled; the mobile path keeps the surface and bandwidth cost down.
DevtoolsDisabled by default on this path; the inspector is a desktop tool.
OrientationActivity configuration changes keep the instance; layout reflows on resize.
RendererGLES 3.0 through the same DonkehWindow, layout and GLRenderer pipeline.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Framework-owned activityZero app boilerplate, but the app cannot subclass or replace the launcher without writing its own host.
Reflection into SDL bindingsKeeps the JNI bootstrap working, but a binding rename is a compile-time-adjacent runtime failure.
Density with a fallbackCorrect CSS pixels on most devices, with a heuristic for SDL builds that already scale the view.
Any-of permission resultPractical for paired permissions, but cannot tell the app which individual name failed.
Fixed 60 Hz / no MSAAPredictable thermal and bandwidth behaviour, at the cost of high-refresh devices and smoother edges.
Manifest still app-ownedPermissions must be declared as well as requested; a missing manifest entry fails at runtime.
No devtools pathSaves layout and renderer overhead on mobile, but debugging happens on desktop or through logging.

topics.summary:
Donkeh.Windowing.Browser is a DOM host, not a renderer. It
mounts the same UILab application, then mirrors the reconciled virtual tree
into real browser elements. CSS layout, focus, carets, selection, scrolling,
form controls and pseudo-classes stay with the browser; the host only keeps
the DOM in sync and forwards events to the same delegates a desktop host
would invoke.

sections.title: Bootstrap
sections.text:
DonkehBrowser.RunAsync creates a default Blazor WebAssembly
host, registers DomHost as a singleton and starts it. Blazor is
used only for its WebAssembly runtime and JavaScript interop. No Blazor
components are rendered; UILab owns the UI tree.
DomHost.StartAsync discovers the [AppRoot],
imports an embedded JavaScript module, initializes it against the container
element, installs the browser permission provider, applies the merged
stylesheet and title, subscribes to Renderer.AfterUpdate,
mounts the component tree and performs the first sync.
The bridge is an embedded ES module
The JavaScript lives in the framework assembly and is imported as a
data:text/javascript;base64,... URL. Apps do not need a
wwwroot folder, static web asset manifest or _content
path. The bridge is a framework concern, not an app packaging detail.

sections.title: Stable ids and snapshots
sections.text:
Every virtual node gets a stable integer id the first time it is synced. The
browser stores the same id on its DOM node, and the C# host keeps both
directions:
StatePurpose
Node → intStable identity for patching, even across keyed reorders.
int → NodeResolves the handler and target for an incoming browser event.
NodeSnapshotLast applied tag, text, attribute map, event list, child order and folded text content.
Root child idsTracks the flattened top-level order, with fragments removed from the DOM shape.
A sync walks the live tree, compares each node with its snapshot and emits
only changed patches. Fragments have no DOM counterpart, so their children
occupy the fragment’s slot in the parent. Nodes that disappear from the walk
are removed from the maps and get a remove patch. The DOM node is never
recreated just because its position changed.
Renderer.AfterUpdate
└── RequestSync (coalesced)
└── SyncAsync
├── walk live tree, assign ids on first sight
├── diff text / attrs / events / children / folded text
├── collect removals
└── serialize DomPatchBatch → JS apply()

sections.title: The patch protocol
sections.text:
The patch vocabulary is deliberately small. The browser owns the real DOM;
the host only describes how it differs from the last applied snapshot.
PatchEffect
createCreate an element or text node with a stable id.
removeRemove a node and forget its id.
childrenSet the exact child order, inserting and moving existing nodes instead of rebuilding.
textReplace a text node’s value.
contentSet folded element text, or clear it when real children return.
attrsReplace the full attribute map; the bridge preserves its own data-donkeh-* bookkeeping.
eventsReplace the event-name list stored on the element for delegation.
Patches are serialized with a source-generated JsonSerializerContext,
which keeps the bridge trim-safe in published WebAssembly builds. The JS side
applies them in order and maintains a Map<number, Node>.
It also handles the cases where the DOM’s live state must win:
- A focused text input keeps the user’s live value unless the virtual tree changed it to a different value.
- value, checked and selected are mirrored as properties as well as attributes, without disturbing a caret.
- Removing checked or selected clears the corresponding property.
- data-donkeh-* attributes are reserved for the bridge and never removed by an attribute replacement.

sections.title: Event delegation
sections.text:
The bridge installs one delegated listener per event family on the container,
not one listener per element. Each element carries its event-name list in a
data attribute. When a browser event fires, the bridge walks from the physical
target up to the nearest element that declares a handler for that event, then
calls back into .NET with:
ArgumentMeaning
handlerIdThe nearest virtual element that owns the handler.
targetIdThe deepest virtual node under the physical event target.
eventNameNormalized name such as click, pointerdown, input or change.
x, yElement-local coordinates, scroll deltas or media time, depending on the event.
text, valueKey name, pasted text or control value.
DomHost.HandleEventAsync resolves both ids, updates control state
for input/change/Enter and invokes the same delegate shapes as the desktop
host: typed event-class handlers, parameterless actions, string handlers and
two-float pointer handlers. Each callback builds the matching
Event subclass, so a browser handler sees the same
ClickEvent, KeyDownEvent or ScrollEvent
as a native one. Browser key names are mapped to the desktop names:
Space, Left, Right, Up,
Down, Escape and single letters. A throwing handler
is contained, as it is on desktop.
Scroll and media tracking are opt-in per element. When an element declares
scroll, the bridge records its previous offsets and reports the
delta. Declaring media events attaches play, pause, ended and timeupdate
tracking. Both use passive listeners where possible.

sections.title: What the browser owns
sections.text:
The browser path intentionally does not run LayoutLab or the OpenGL renderer.
It delegates far more to the platform than the desktop host:
ConcernOwner
CSS layout, cascade and pseudo-classesThe browser.
Focus, caret, selection and IMEThe browser’s native form controls.
Scrolling and scrollbarsThe browser; the host consumes scroll deltas.
img, video, audioNative browser elements and media APIs.
canvasThe element exists, but no C# draw callback is wired.
InspectorNot part of the browser host; devtools are desktop-only.

sections.title: Browser permissions
sections.text:
BrowserPermissionService forwards the supported capabilities to
the embedded module, which uses the corresponding browser API:
PermissionBrowser mechanism
CameragetUserMedia({ video: true }); the temporary stream is stopped immediately.
MicrophonegetUserMedia({ audio: true }); same stop-after-check policy.
Locationnavigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition with a 15-second timeout.
NotificationsNotification.requestPermission(), with existing grant/deny states short-circuited.
Storagenavigator.storage.persist().
MotionDeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission() where available; otherwise true.
ClipboardA clipboard read, which requires a user gesture in most browsers.
Photos, contacts, calendar, BluetoothUnsupported; returns false.
User gesture required
Browsers gate camera, microphone, clipboard and some notification prompts on
a user gesture. Calling Host.Permissions.Camera() from a button
click works; calling it during startup may be rejected even though the same
API succeeds later. Failures resolve false rather than throwing.

sections.title: Why the bridge stays small
sections.text:
- Stable ids. Keyed reorders move existing DOM nodes; they do not recreate subtrees or lose browser focus.
- Snapshot diffs. Only changed text, attributes, events and child orders cross the interop boundary.
- Coalesced sync. Multiple renderer updates in flight collapse into one drain loop; the newest tree wins.
- Delegated events. One listener per event family on the container, not per element.
- No layout engine. The browser performs layout and paint; the host never builds boxes or instructions.
- Trim-safe JSON. Source-generated serialization avoids reflection metadata in published WASM builds.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
DOM is authoritativeNative form behaviour is excellent, but the host must reconcile browser-driven value changes back into virtual node state.
No layout engineBrowser CSS and layout do the real work, so desktop-specific layout behaviour and the inspector are unavailable.
Data-URL moduleNo app packaging requirements, but the bridge is loaded as a generated module rather than a cacheable static asset.
Full attribute replacementSimple and correct, but every attribute map crosses the interop boundary when any attribute changes.
Delegated eventsOne listener setup, but every event walks ancestors to find a handler.
No canvas drawingNative canvas exists, but C# callbacks are not bridged; there is no WebGL interop yet.
Permission gesture rulesApps must trigger prompts from interaction; startup checks can fail for reasons the host cannot control.
WASM startup and trimmingThe Blazor runtime is large compared with a native host; source-generated JSON and rooting keep the bridge safe under trimming.

topics.title: CLI tool
topics.summary:
Donkeh.CliTool is the donkeh global tool. It is
deliberately small: parse a handful of commands, generate a project or a
component, wire platform targets into an SDK-style project, and get out of the
way. It never evaluates MSBuild, never runs a restore implicitly, and does not
own a template engine.

sections.title: Command surface
sections.text:
Program.cs is a one-line entry point that returns
Cli.Run(args). The CLI catches CliException and
unexpected exceptions alike, prints error: … to stderr and
returns exit code 1. Success paths return 0. There is no stack trace or
partial stack of console noise on a normal user mistake.

code.label: Terminal
code.content:
donkeh new project [<directory>] [--name <name>] [--type application|framework] [--framework <path>] [--force]
donkeh new component <name> [--project <path>] [--force]
donkeh enable-target <desktop|android|web> [--project <path>]
donkeh enable-feature <hot-reload> [--project <path>]
donkeh watch [--project <path>] [-- <app args>]
donkeh upgrade project [--version <version>] [--project <path>]
donkeh --help
donkeh --version

sections.title: Argument parsing
sections.text:
ParsedArguments is a small hand-written parser, not
System.CommandLine. It collects positionals, accepts
--option value and --option=value, handles
--force and help flags, and rejects unknown options or missing
values with a clean message. That keeps startup tiny and avoids a dependency
whose help formatting would be larger than the tool.
InputBehaviour
new project .Uses the current directory; the project name is derived from that folder.
new project MyAppCreates MyApp/ and names the project MyApp.
--name Acme.AppOverrides the project name and therefore the root namespace.
--forceAllows overwriting generated files; without it an existing target is an error.
--helpPrints command-specific help and exits 0.

sections.title: Checkout or NuGet
sections.text:
FrameworkLocator decides whether a new project should reference a
local framework checkout or the published packages:
- An explicit --framework must resolve to a directory containing Build/Donkeh.props or a repository root with a Donkeh folder; otherwise it is an error.
- Without one, the locator walks up from the current directory and then the tool's base directory looking for the same markers.
- If nothing is found, it returns null and the generator uses NuGet packages.
A checkout project imports Build/Donkeh.props and
Build/Donkeh.targets, uses project references, and carries a
generated Directory.Build.targets. A NuGet project has no
framework import; it references Donkeh.Windowing at the CLI's own
assembly version and leaves the framework's package build assets to supply the
entry point.
No restore during generation
The CLI writes files and prints the next command. It does not run
dotnet restore, so generation stays fast and does not fail because
of a transient network or credential problem. dotnet run or
dotnet restore performs the restore when the developer is ready.

sections.title: Project generation
sections.text:
ProjectGenerator creates the project file, Program.cs
and .gitignore, plus the checkout targets file when needed. The
generated app is intentionally minimal:
DecisionReason
Project name from folderdonkeh new project . uses the containing directory name, so a normal folder does not need a second argument.
Invalid filename characters replaced with _The project name becomes a file name and a namespace; sanitising here prevents a later failure.
Version from the tool assemblyA released CLI references the matching package version; the generated file exposes DonkehVersion so it can be overridden.
No MainThe framework package or checkout build targets generate the entry point from [AppRoot].
No CSS fileThe blank project has no component folder yet; new component adds one with its own stylesheet.

Program.cs

sections.title: Framework projects
sections.text:
--type framework generates a component library and a console
test container instead of a standalone app. The library is packable, the
container references it directly, and the container discovers every public
component in the library assembly and renders it in a gallery.
Acme.Components/
├── Acme.Components.sln
├── src/
│   ├── Acme.Components.csproj     // packable library
│   └── Components/
│       └── HelloCard/
│           ├── HelloCard.cs
│           └── HelloCard.css
├── test-container/
│   ├── TestContainer.csproj       // executable, references ../src
│   ├── Program.cs                 // AppRoot + reflection gallery
│   └── Styles/
│       └── gallery.css
├── .gitignore
└── README.md
The library references Donkeh.UILab; the container references
Donkeh.Windowing and the library. In checkout mode the library
references the checkout's UILab project directly, while the container imports
the normal framework props and targets. The container walks the library
assembly for non-abstract components with a public parameterless constructor
and uses C(type) to mount each one.
The generated README records the same preview and publish commands. Adding a
component with donkeh new component from the project root does
not currently target the library automatically; pass
--project src/Acme.Components.csproj, or run the command from
src/.

code.label: Terminal
code.content:
donkeh new project Acme.Components --type framework
cd Acme.Components
donkeh enable-feature hot-reload
donkeh watch

# publish when ready
dotnet pack src/Acme.Components.csproj -c Release

sections.title: Component generation
sections.text:
new component FileList finds the project, reads its
RootNamespace, normalises the component name and writes one folder
per component:
src/
└── Components/
└── FileList/
├── FileList.cs
└── FileList.css
The generated class uses the typed HtmlHelper builder and
registers its stylesheet with an assembly attribute:
The component namespace is RootNamespace + ".Components" unless
the root namespace already ends with .Components. The CSS class
is the PascalCase name converted to kebab case, including acronym handling such
as MyHTTPClient → my-http-client. Existing files are
refused unless --force is passed.

sections.title: Formatting-preserving project edits
sections.text:
CsprojEditor does not deserialize and reserialize the project.
It detects the file's line ending, checks whether the resource path is already
present with either slash style, and inserts a small ItemGroup
immediately before the final </Project>. Comments,
formatting, ordering and unrelated properties survive unchanged, and the
operation is idempotent.
The generator resolves namespaces through XDocument when the file
is valid XML, but falls back to the project file name if parsing fails. That
keeps a messy but buildable project editable without making XML parsing a hard
requirement.

code.label: Added item
code.content:
<ItemGroup>
  <EmbeddedResource Include="src/Components/FileList/FileList.css" />
</ItemGroup>

sections.title: Target wiring
sections.text:
enable-target detects checkout versus NuGet mode by looking for
Donkeh.props in the project text, then edits the appropriate
surface:
TargetCheckout projectNuGet project
desktopAlready enabled; the command reports that the target is already enabled.Already enabled; the generated project already targets net10.0.
androidEnables <DonkehAndroid>true, uncommenting the template flag when present.Adds net10.0-android, SupportedOSPlatformVersion 24 and a conditional Donkeh.Windowing.Android reference.
webEnables <DonkehWeb>true.Adds net10.0-browser, browser-wasm RIDs, the browser host, the Blazor package and the WebAssembly SDK pack.
The edits are regular-expression and text based, not MSBuild-aware. They
preserve the existing TargetFramework or append to
TargetFrameworks, add properties inside the first
PropertyGroup and add conditional PackageReference
items before the closing project tag. Enabling an already-enabled target is a
clean error instead of a silent no-op.

sections.title: Names and sanitising
sections.text:
Identifiers provides the small amount of naming policy the CLI
needs. Component names split on spaces, hyphens, underscores, dots and path
separators, then PascalCase each word. C# keywords gain a
Component suffix, names starting with a digit get an underscore,
and namespaces PascalCase each dotted segment. Kebab case inserts hyphens at
case boundaries, including acronym-to-word transitions.

sections.title: Development features and watch
sections.text:
enable-feature hot-reload adds the optional CSS watcher to the
executable project:
A framework root resolves to its test-container project. A
framework checkout receives a conditional ProjectReference;
a NuGet project receives a conditional PackageReference. Both
carry '$(Configuration)' == 'Debug', so Release builds and
published applications do not reference or copy the watcher. The same item
group marks embedded CSS with Watch="false" so a stylesheet
save does not make dotnet watch rebuild. The command is
idempotent.
donkeh watch refuses to start until the feature is enabled,
then runs dotnet watch run -c Debug -f net10.0 with
DONKEH_HOT_RELOAD=1. Arguments after -- are
forwarded to the application. Supported C# edits are applied in place by
the .NET Hot Reload agent; the development package detects the source
change, waits for the patch to settle and re-renders every mounted
component. A second refresh covers a slower patch. Unsupported edits make
dotnet watch restart the app. CSS edits rebuild the cascade
through the in-process stylesheet reloader instead of a build.

code.label: Terminal
code.content:
donkeh enable-feature hot-reload
donkeh watch

sections.title: Upgrading a project
sections.text:
donkeh upgrade project moves a NuGet-based project to a newer
Donkeh package set and updates the installed CLI:
- Clears all NuGet caches with dotnet nuget locals all --clear.
- Updates DonkehVersion and any literal Donkeh.* package versions in the project.
- Runs dotnet restore --force --no-cache so the packages are downloaded fresh.
- Runs dotnet tool update --global Donkeh.CliTool --version ....
A project generated against a local framework checkout is rejected; upgrade
the checkout with git instead. If the global tool is locked because it is the
process running the command, the update is scheduled for after the command
exits.

code.label: Terminal
code.content:
donkeh upgrade project --version=1.0.25

# or resolve the latest stable version
donkeh upgrade project

sections.title: Tests
sections.text:
The CLI tests call the generators directly against temporary directories rather
than spawning processes. They cover checkout and NuGet project shapes,
component folder creation and stylesheet registration, target editing,
feature reference selection, force protection and identifier normalisation.
That keeps the feedback loop fast and makes the generated file content part
of the tested contract.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
No MSBuild evaluationFast and dependency-free, but the CLI cannot understand complex property functions or imported target frameworks.
Text-preserving XML editsKeeps projects human-formatted, but assumes conventional SDK-style XML and inserts only at known anchors.
Version from the tool assemblyReleased tools align with packages automatically; a locally built CLI with a dev version may need DonkehVersion overridden.
No implicit restore/runGeneration stays fast and offline-capable, at the cost of one explicit next command.
Folder-per-component conventionPredictable and organised, but a project that intentionally keeps flat component files is not supported by the generator.
Regex-based target editsSmall and readable, but unusual project structures may need manual edits.
No uninstall/removal commandGeneration is additive; deleting a component is a normal file operation, not a CLI feature.

files without taking ownership of them.
