topics.title: Data
topics.summary:
Donkeh.Data is deliberately generic. It does not know how to
parse CSS and it does not know how to paint; it describes the relationships
between tokens, selectors, declarations and conditions. The representation is
a set of flat tables whose columns are almost entirely integer ids into
interned values or other tables.

sections.title: The core idea: relationships as ids
sections.text:
A stylesheet is a graph: a selector owns declarations, a declaration
references a property and a value, a rule may be gated by a condition, and a
condition may be nested inside another. The obvious object model gives every
node a class and every edge a reference. That is pleasant to debug and
expensive to hold in memory.
Donkeh stores the graph as parallel lists. A rule is a Rule
value with five integers: selector id, property id, value id, condition id
and layer id. A selector record points into a shared token arena. A condition
is a compiled delegate plus a parent id. There are no per-rule objects, no
per-selector token arrays and no string fields in the hot structures.
A rule is 20 bytes. Every negative id is an absent optional edge. Resolving a
rule to text is a lookup in InternTable, not a pointer chase
through a tree of small heap objects. The table itself is append-only while
parsing, so ids are dense, stable and safe to use as array indices.

code.label: Rule
code.content:
public readonly struct Rule
{
    public required int SelectorId { get; init; }  // -> DataTable.Selectors
    public required int PropertyId { get; init; }  // -> interned "background-color"
    public required int ValueId    { get; init; }  // -> interned "#fff"
    public int ConditionId { get; init; } = -1;    // -> DataTable.Conditions
    public int LayerId     { get; init; } = -1;    // -> DataTable.Layers
}

sections.title: What lives in the table
sections.text:
TableRecordPurpose
SelectorsSelectorRecordToken-arena slice, primary discriminator, packed specificity, compound slice, matchable flag, pseudo-element.
RulesRuleDeclaration edges: selector, property, value, condition and layer ids.
ConditionsConditionCompiled predicate, parent id and shared executor id.
Imports, Namespaces, Layers, Scopessmall id recordsAt-rule metadata preserved for the host and cascade ordering.
Keyframes, Descriptors, MarginBoxes, Charsetssmall id recordsKeyframe stops and descriptor blocks without attaching them to normal selectors.
Selector / condition token arenasToken[]One flat token buffer for all selectors and one for all condition preludes.
Compound / filter / pseudo arenasvalue recordsSelector analysis stored once, so matching never re-parses selector tokens.
The SelectorRecord is the best example of the pattern. It does not
own its tokens or compounds. It stores TokenOffset and
TokenLength into the table's selector-token arena, plus
CompoundOffset and CompoundCount into the compound
arena. Attribute filters and pseudo classes are similarly sliced out of
table-wide arenas. A table with thousands of selectors has a handful of large
arrays instead of thousands of small ones.
Arenas and intrusive lists
Collision chains are not List<int> per hash bucket. The
table keeps a dictionary from key to head id and a parallel
_next list; the head is the newest entry and every record points
at the previous one. Selector hash buckets, condition buckets, executor
buckets, discriminator buckets, attribute-name buckets and per-selector rule
chains all use the same trick. That removes one allocation per bucket and
keeps traversal inside two contiguous arrays.
_discriminatorHeads: { key → newest selector id }
│
├── selector 42 → selector 17 → selector 9 → -1
│        _discriminatorNext[42] = 17
│        _discriminatorNext[17] = 9
│        _discriminatorNext[9]  = -1
└── key = (TokenKind.Identifier, interned "btn")

sections.title: Why it is small
sections.text:
The memory benchmark reports a 7.46× improvement over the
object-per-node representation. The saving is structural, not a micro
optimisation:
- Values, not objects. A rule is a 20-byte struct in one list; there is no object header, no reference field and no per-rule allocation.
- Strings are interned once. Repeated properties and values such as color, display, 0, block and #fff are one id each, regardless of how many declarations use them.
- Selectors share arenas. Tokens live in one buffer. A selector record is an offset/length pair, not a token array.
- Analysis is stored once. Compounds, parsed attribute filters, pseudo records and the An+B values are produced when a selector is interned, not re-derived per match.
- Identical selectors are deduplicated. .a .b written twice is one selector with two rules; whitespace around explicit combinators normalises to the same token sequence.
- Executors are shared. The same media query under different parents compiles once; condition records differ only by parent id and delegate reference.
- Adjacent duplicate rules collapse. A flattened selector list that produces the same declaration twice stores it once when it is adjacent in source order.
RecordApproximate sizeWhat dominates
Rule20 BFive 32-bit ids.
Token12 BKind, interned text id, packed 24-bit start + 8-bit length.
Conditiondelegate ref + 8 BShared ConditionFunction, parent id, executor id.
AttributeFilter~12 BName id, value id, byte operator, bool flag.
PseudoRecord~20 BKind, An+B terms and :not() argument slice.
On Bootstrap 5.3.8 the pipeline sees 232,108 characters, 46,438 tokens,
2,762 unique selectors, 6,496 rules and 18 conditions. Build time is roughly
13 ms in the debugger’s release run, with 2.4 MB of transient allocation for
tokens and parsing. Those allocations are the build cost; the flattened table
is what survives.

sections.title: Conditions are delegates
sections.text:
Condition is where the design becomes unusually direct. A
condition does not store an expression tree, an operator enum or a list of
feature values to interpret later. It stores a compiled
ConditionFunction:
The compiler is called once per distinct prelude. Media queries become a
small immutable closure that compares fields on
RendererContext; @supports and
@container can be supplied by a different compiler. The rule
builder stores the resulting delegate reference and a condition id. At match
time the engine calls the delegate  -  there is no re-parsing and no
interpretation of the query text.
MechanismWhy it is fast
Compile once per preludeThe token scan, feature parsing and closure creation happen during stylesheet build, not per node.
Shared executorsConditions are interned by (tokens, parent); executors are interned by tokens alone, so a responsive query compiles once even when nested in many scopes.
Delegate call per conditionbool (in RendererContext) is a direct call with no allocation and no virtual expression walk.
Parent-chain short circuitA nested rule evaluates its innermost condition and stops at the first failure.
Version-stamped cacheResults are memoised per table and RendererContext.Version; every rule sharing a query pays for it once per environment change.
Fail closedA missing compiler, a null result or a thrown exception becomes AlwaysFalse, never an accidental match.
Condition.AlwaysTrue and AlwaysFalse are static
delegates, and AlwaysTrueCompiler is useful for tests and for
builds that do not need media-query filtering. The cache is deliberately
conservative: a new context instance or a changed version invalidates it, so
results are never shared across environments.

code.label: ConditionFunction

sections.title: Selector analysis at intern time
sections.text:
Interning a selector is the expensive moment, and it happens once. A single
pass splits the token sequence into compounds on combinators and descendant
gaps, tracks bracket/parenthesis depth so operators inside
[attr^=v] and :nth-child() are not mistaken for
combinators, parses attribute filters and pseudo classes, and computes
specificity.
- Specificity is packed into one integer: 10 bits for ids, 10 for classes/attributes/pseudo-classes and 10 for types. It is computed once and read as an integer during sorting.
- The right-most token becomes the PrimaryDiscriminator, normalised so identifiers, property names and function names share one bucket.
- IsMatchable is false for unsupported constructs. The selector is still stored for inspection, but matching never returns a wrong positive.
- ::before/::after are recorded separately, letting the host skip generated-content matching entirely when a sheet never uses it.
- Selectors whose subject is an attribute selector are indexed by the attribute name; structural pseudo-class subjects go into a small unkeyed list.
This is why matching does not have to re-tokenize or re-analyze anything. The
selector record already contains the plan: compounds, filters, pseudo
records, combinator links and specificity.

sections.title: Matching as a table lookup
sections.text:
MatchRules does not scan every selector. It collects candidate
ids from the node's own interned keys:
- id, tag name, every class name and the universal bucket;
- attribute-name buckets for selectors whose subject is an attribute;
- the small list of structural pseudo-class subjects.
Every probe is an integer dictionary lookup and an intrusive-list walk. The
subject compound is verified first, then the selector is walked right to left
through the compound plan. Only after a selector matches are its rules walked
through the per-selector rule chain. Conditions are filtered last, so a rule
gated by a media query does not pay for the condition until its selector has
already matched.
The result is sorted weakest first: layer order, then specificity, then source
order. Applying rules in that order lets later declarations win exactly as
the cascade requires. The span overload writes into a caller-provided buffer
and reuses table scratch lists, which is the allocation-free path used by the
renderer.
Bootstrap 5.3.8 measurementResult
Stylesheet232,108 characters, 46,438 tokens
Selectors / rules / conditions2,762 / 6,496 / 18
Build time~13 ms, ~17.7 MB/s, 2.4 MB transient allocation
Matching a 4,512-element page~4.25 µs/node, ~56,500 matches per pass
Hot leaf / cold leaf~8.25 µs (53 matches) / ~3.54 µs (1 match)
Retained-memory benchmark7.46× improvement over the object-per-node baseline

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Ids instead of referencesEvery debugging session needs the intern table to turn an id back into text. Id 0 is a valid token; -1 is the absent sentinel.
Flat arenasGrowing an arena invalidates previously returned spans. Re-read through GetSelectorSpan instead of caching the span.
Append-only recordsThere is no general deletion. The inspector can edit a rule value or property in place; removing a selector would invalidate ids and is not supported.
Global intern tableStable ids for the process, but the table grows with distinct text and is never evicted.
Shared scratch buffersMatching is not re-entrant and the table is not thread-safe while being mutated.
Build-time allocationThe flattened result is compact, but parsing and interning still allocate tokens, lists and distinct strings. The 2.4 MB Bootstrap number is transient build cost.
Fail-closed conditionsAn unsupported query silently disables its rules. That is safer than applying styles the engine cannot verify, but it can look like a missing rule.

sections.title: Code tour
sections.text:
FileRead it for…
Data/Source/DataTable.csAll tables, arenas, candidate indexes and the condition cache.
Data/Source/DataTable.Matching.csCandidate collection, right-to-left selector verification and cascade ordering.
Data/Source/Rule.csThe 20-byte declaration edge.
Data/Source/SelectorRecord.csThe selector slice and packed specificity.
Data/Source/Dom/SelectorAnalysis.csOne-pass compound splitting, filter parsing, pseudo parsing and specificity.
Data/Source/Dom/SelectorPlan.csCompound, combinator and pseudo records stored in shared arenas.
Data/Source/Condition.csConditionFunction, shared executors and fail-closed defaults.
DataEngine/Source/MediaConditionCompiler.csThe media-query compiler that produces the delegate.
The short version: the parser gives Data a stream of interned tokens; Data turns
those tokens into a compact relationship graph of integer edges. Matching then
works almost entirely by indexing, filtering and calling already-compiled
predicates, rather than by interpreting a stylesheet-shaped object graph.

topics.title: DataEngine
topics.summary:
Donkeh.DataEngine is the bridge between a token list and the
flat DataTable. It is a single forward pass over tokens:
no source text ownership, no AST, no backtracking, no re-tokenization.
It also owns the condition-compiler hook that turns a query prelude into a
predicate for the table.

sections.title: What the engine owns
sections.text:
The parser below this layer has already removed whitespace and comments and
classified every token. DataEngine’s job is structural: decide whether a
token run is a rule, a declaration, an at-rule, a nested rule or a
descriptor, then write ids into the table. The source string is not retained,
and selector or condition token sequences are copied into the table’s arenas
so the returned table is independent of the token list.
CSS text
└── Tokenizer.Parse
└── List<Token>          (borrowed, never owned)
└── CssStreamParser
├── StreamContext     condition / container / rule frames
├── selector composer parent × child flattening
├── text buffer       property/value/interning scratch
└── DataTable         selectors, rules, conditions, metadata
└── ConditionCompiler once per distinct prelude
DataEngine itself is tiny and immutable. It stores one
ConditionCompiler and exposes three entry points:
Build(string), Build(List<Token>) and
Build(List<Token>, DataTable). The last one appends several
stylesheets into the same table, preserving call order for the cascade.
No compiler means AlwaysFalseCompiler, so gated rules fail closed
rather than applying by accident.

sections.title: A ref struct, one pass
sections.text:
CssStreamParser is a ref struct that borrows the
token span and the destination table. It is stack-only, cannot cross an
await, and owns a pooled character buffer that must be returned.
That shape is deliberate: it keeps the parser allocation-light while making
the lifetime of its borrowed inputs explicit.
StatePurpose
_tokensBorrowed token span. Original source offsets survive so gaps can be detected.
_tableDestination table, mutated in place.
_compilerInvoked once per distinct condition prelude.
StreamContextNested condition, container and rule frames plus a flat selector stack.
_layerStackCascade layers currently entered, outermost first.
_composerReused token buffer for parent/child selector composition.
_selectorScratchSelector ids for one rule, de-duplicated with a linear scan.
_textBufferArrayPool-backed scratch for property and value normalisation.
The constructor rents 256 characters from
ArrayPool<char>.Shared; Dispose returns it.
Everything else is reused across the stylesheet, including the selector
composer and the selector-id scratch list. The table is pre-sized from
tokens.Count / 8 so most growth reallocations are avoided
without keeping a per-token buffer.

sections.title: Blocks, statements and local recovery
sections.text:
Parse calls ParseBlock(topLevel: true), which loops
until EOF. A } closes a non-top-level block; stray closing braces
at top level are consumed and ignored. Semicolons at block level are skipped.
At-keywords go to ParseAtRule; everything else goes to
ParseSegment.
ParseSegment first checks for a custom property declaration
(--name:) before looking for the rule/declaration split. That
ordering matters because a custom-property value may contain braces, and it
must not be mistaken for a nested rule. Otherwise
FindHeaderEnd scans for the first top-level {,
; or }:
TerminatorInterpretation
{A style rule; the prelude is the selector list and the block is parsed recursively.
; or }A declaration or malformed segment; declaration parsing or local skip recovery.
EOFEnd of input; a truncated statement is abandoned.
Error recovery is intentionally local and silent. A malformed declaration is
skipped to the next top-level ;, { or },
parenthesis- and bracket-aware so a semicolon inside url(...) or
an attribute selector does not end the skip. A malformed selector prelude
still consumes its block, but pushes a container frame that hides the enclosing
selector, so declarations cannot leak onto the parent. An at-rule whose
prelude ends at EOF or at a closing brace is abandoned without consuming the
brace. No parse exception is reported to the caller.

sections.title: At-rules and the condition chain
sections.text:
ParseAtRule finds the prelude terminator first. A semicolon
terminates statement at-rules; a brace starts a block; EOF or an enclosing
closing brace abandons the at-rule. Block at-rules are dispatched in a fixed
order:
- @nest  -  parsed as a nested style rule.
- Conditions  -  @media, @supports, @container, @document, @-moz-document, @starting-style.
- @keyframes and @-webkit-keyframes.
- @scope, @layer.
- @page margin boxes and descriptor at-rules.
- An unknown container, traversed with the selector context hidden.
Only condition blocks keep the enclosing selector context. A rule inside
@media therefore inherits the selector of the rule it is nested
in; a rule inside @layer, @scope or an unknown
container does not accidentally attach declarations to the parent. Conditions
call DataTable.GetOrAddCondition with the current condition id as
the parent, so nesting becomes an AND chain.
The parser stores the outermost condition id on each rule. Evaluation walks
the parent chain and stops at the first failure. Conditions are interned by
(tokens, parent), while executors are interned by tokens alone,
so the same media query nested under different parents shares one compiled
delegate. The engine never interprets the query text during matching.

code.label: Nested conditions

sections.title: Selector list flattening and nesting
sections.text:
ParseRule splits a selector prelude on commas that are not inside
parentheses or brackets, so :is(.a, .b) and
[data-x="a,b"] stay intact. Each branch is flattened against
every selector of the enclosing rule. At the root the branch is interned
verbatim; inside a nested rule the result is the cartesian product of parent
and child selectors, followed by a linear de-duplication pass because selector
lists are short.
Compose preserves CSS nesting semantics. A child without
& becomes a descendant of the parent. Each &
is replaced in place by the entire parent selector. Whitespace is reconstructed
as a synthetic gap, so & .a stays a descendant while
&.a stays one compound. A leading & never
introduces a leading gap. Composed tokens are copied into the table before the
next pair, so the composer buffer can be reused for the entire stylesheet.
If no selector survives flattening, the block is still consumed as a container
so the token stream stays synchronized. That is the same “hide the parent”
rule used for malformed rule headers.

code.label: Nesting

sections.title: Declarations and normalization
sections.text:
ParseDeclaration locates the top-level colon with
FindColon, then scans the value with FindValueEnd.
Both scans track parentheses, square brackets and  -  for values  -  balanced
curly braces, so function arguments, attribute selectors and custom-property
blocks do not terminate early. The parser then chooses one of four paths:
ContextDestination
Descriptor at-ruleCssDescriptor, or CssMarginBox inside an @page margin box.
Inside @keyframesOne CssKeyframe per current keyframe selector, with the condition id.
No selector or empty valueDiscarded without interning.
Normal style ruleOne Rule per selector id, carrying property, value, condition and layer ids.
Property names are ASCII-lower-cased unless they are custom properties.
Values preserve case because CSS values can be case-sensitive. Token text is
written into the pooled character buffer with one space wherever the original
source had a gap; comments and whitespace never appear as tokens, so a gap is
simply previous.EndIndex < current.StartIndex. A single-token
property or value whose interned text already has the right casing reuses its
existing id and never touches the buffer.
The cheap path is the common path
Most declarations are one property token and one value token. The
NormalizeAndIntern fast path checks for exactly one token and
returns its interned id directly. Multi-token values such as
0 8px 16px rgba(0,0,0,.2) pay for normalization once, then all
repeated uses share the resulting id.

sections.title: Layers, keyframes and descriptors
Performance and allocation
sections.text:
The engine is built around reuse and one-way movement. There is no AST to
allocate, no backtracking cursor to reset and no per-selector token array. The
only large temporary is the token list produced by the tokenizer; the parser
itself reuses its composer, selector scratch, layer stack and pooled text
buffer.
Bootstrap 5.3.8Result
Input232,108 characters, 46,438 tokens
Output2,762 selectors, 6,496 rules, 18 conditions, 8 keyframes, 1 charset
Tokenize + build~13 ms total, ~17.7 MB/s
Transient allocation~2.4 MB for tokens, parsing and interning
GC collections0 / 0 / 0 in the debugger run
Tokenizer-only baseline~5.5 ms of the ~13 ms total
The benchmark suite scales the same pipeline over 1M, 4M and 16M character
synthetic corpora, with a second corpus that repeats selectors and conditions
to stress identity lookup and dedup. The query benchmarks separately measure
rule scans, discriminator lookups and cached versus invalidated condition
evaluation, so build cost and match cost are not conflated.
Where build time goes
Selector interning is the expensive part of a build: hashing tokens,
analysing compounds, parsing attribute filters and pseudo classes, and
deduplicating selector ids. Declaration parsing is comparatively cheap,
especially when the single-token normalization fast path applies. More
selectors per rule and deep nesting increase the cartesian product and
therefore the interning work.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Single forward pass, no ASTVery little temporary structure, but debugging is token-index based and there is no rich parse tree to inspect.
Local recovery, no diagnosticsMalformed sections are skipped or hidden; nothing is reported to the caller. A typo can look like a missing rule.
Table mutation is eagerThe table is complete only when the parse finishes successfully; there is no rollback if a later section fails.
ref struct parserStack-only and allocation-light, but cannot be stored in a field, used across await or shared between threads.
Condition compiler is injectedMedia queries are supported by one compiler; @supports and @container need a host-supplied compiler or fail closed.
Nesting is flattened at build timeMatching stays simple, but deeply nested selector lists can multiply quickly before deduplication.
Normalization is pooled, not freeMulti-token values copy into the text buffer; repeated values then share one interned id.

sections.text:
FileRead it for…

DataEngine/Source/CssStreamParser.csThe entire forward-only parser: blocks, at-rules, rules, nesting, declarations, recovery and normalization.
Data/Source/StreamContext.csCondition/container/rule frames and the flat selector stack used for nesting.

The mental model is a one-way funnel: the tokenizer decides what each token
is; DataEngine decides how tokens relate structurally; Data stores those
relationships as integer edges and makes them queryable. Nothing in the
pipeline goes back to the source text after tokenization.

topics.title: Hosting
topics.summary:
Donkeh.Hosting is the small, platform-neutral contract every
host shares. It does not open windows or render anything. It discovers the
application root, carries the settings that native hosts need, and exposes
the platform flags and awaitable permission surface that app code can use
without referencing a specific host implementation.

sections.title: What belongs here
sections.text:
The package deliberately has no dependency on Silk.NET, OpenGL, LibVLC or a
native window. That is what lets the same app assembly compile for desktop,
Android and the browser. A few types live here even though their namespaces
belong to other packages, precisely so settings can describe a platform
feature without pulling the implementation into every consumer:
TypeWhy it lives in Hosting
AppRootAttributeDeclares the root component and all host settings in one place.
AppRootDefinitionCarries the discovered root factory, merged stylesheet and settings to any host.
WindowSettingsPlatform-neutral window description; the native host applies it.
RenderPathLets settings select direct or indirect rendering without referencing the GL renderer.
DevToolsDockLets settings choose an inspector position without referencing the inspector implementation.
Host / HostPermissionsThe app-facing platform and permission API.

sections.title: The attributed app root
sections.text:
An application declares one component:
The attribute is the whole application contract. It carries window size,
title, frame style, VSync, frame cap, clear colour, MSAA samples, render
path, DPI override, resizability, min/max size, icon, topmost and transparency
flags, inspector settings, and an optional native corner radius.
ToWindowSettings() converts those constants into the mutable
struct a native host consumes.
Attribute arguments are constants
C# attributes cannot take object initializers, so settings are named
properties. CornerRadius uses float.NaN to mean
“derive the window shape from CSS”; zero means a square frameless window.
Zero is also a sentinel for several native settings, so prefer
WindowSettings.Default over default when building
settings in code.

code.label: App.cs
App.cs

sections.title: Discovery
sections.text:
AppRootLocator.Find() is the single discovery point used by
every platform entry point. It checks the entry assembly first, then every
loaded assembly. The first type with [AppRoot] wins.
- The type must derive from Component.
- It must not be abstract.
- It must expose a public parameterless constructor.
Failures are explicit: a missing root, a non-component type, or a missing
constructor throws an InvalidOperationException with a message
that names the type. The attribute is not inherited, so a derived component
does not accidentally become a second root.
For migration, the locator falls back to the legacy
[DonkehApp]/IDonkehApp contract when no
[AppRoot] is present. New applications should use the
attribute; the legacy path exists so older projects keep compiling.

sections.title: The app definition
sections.text:
Discovery produces an AppRootDefinition: the component type,
the converted WindowSettings, the merged author stylesheet and
a factory that creates the root component node. The stylesheet is loaded
during definition construction through Stylesheet.Load(), so
reflection and embedded-resource reads happen once at startup rather than
per frame.
AppRootLocator.Find()
└── AppRootDefinition
├── ComponentType     [AppRoot] type, or null for legacy
├── Settings          WindowSettings copy
├── Styles            merged embedded CSS
└── CreateRoot()      _.C(componentType)
Hosts consume the definition differently but share the same object. The
desktop/browser entry point mounts CreateRoot() into a
Renderer and passes Settings to the window. The
Android activity discovers the same definitions and applies its own surface,
density and lifecycle rules.

sections.title: Window settings
sections.text:
WindowSettings is a mutable struct so it can be composed with
an object initializer and copied into the native window without a heap
allocation. Defaults are desktop-oriented: 1280 × 800, resizable, not
VSync, 144 FPS cap, opaque white clear colour, 4× MSAA, inspector enabled
at the bottom.
GroupFields
GeometryWidth, Height, Min/MaxWidth, Min/MaxHeight, Resizable, Frameless, FullScreen, Maximized, CornerRadius
PresentationVSync, TargetFramesPerSecond, ClearColor, Samples, RenderPath, Transparent, TopMost
IdentityTitle, Icon
ScalingDpiScale; zero derives the ratio from the framebuffer, mobile hosts set display density explicitly
Developer toolsEnableDevTools, DevToolsPosition
Settings are copied when the native window is constructed. Changing a copy
afterwards has no effect on the live window, and some values are only
applied at creation. A default(WindowSettings) bypasses the
constructor and produces a fixed, non-resizable window with inspector off
and an uncapped frame rate  -  not the documented defaults.

sections.title: Render path and devtools placement
sections.text:
RenderPath.Auto uses indirect submission when the driver
exposes the required extensions and falls back to direct instanced draws
otherwise. Indirect bakes geometry into one GPU-resident
buffer and submits indirect commands; Direct keeps the same
geometry but issues one instanced draw per batch, which is useful for
benchmarking or isolating driver problems. Browser hosts ignore the value.
DevToolsDock selects bottom, right or a separate native
inspector window. The enum lives in Hosting so settings can reference it
without forcing every consumer to reference Donkeh.Inspector.

sections.title: Platform flags and permissions
sections.text:
Host exposes simple platform predicates:
IsAndroid, IsIOS, IsWindows,
IsMac, IsLinux, IsWeb,
IsDesktop, IsMobile, IsBrowser and a
friendly PlatformName. These are safe on every target and
require no host setup.
Permission checks are intentionally asynchronous because mobile and browser
platforms may need a system prompt:
MechanismBehaviour
Host.PermissionsShared HostPermissions instance with camera, microphone, location, notifications, photos, storage, contacts, calendar, Bluetooth, motion and clipboard helpers.
Grant cacheA granted result is cached for the host lifetime; a denial is not, so the app can retry after a settings change.
In-flight deduplicationConcurrent requests for the same permission share one platform prompt.
CancellationA cancelled prompt resolves to false rather than throwing.
Provider replacementHost.UsePermissions(service) installs the platform provider and clears cached grants; passing null restores the default.
Default providerDesktop grants and lets the device API enforce access; mobile, browser and unknown platforms return false until their host installs a real provider.
Failure policyUnknown permissions, provider exceptions and cancelled prompts all fail closed.
The default is not a security model
The desktop default answers “granted” because .NET has no common runtime
permission prompt. The actual camera, microphone or filesystem operation can
still fail. Mobile and browser hosts are expected to replace the provider
during startup; until they do, permission checks return false.

code.label: Permissions

sections.title: Startup cost and steady state
sections.text:
Hosting is almost entirely startup code. Discovery reflects over loaded
assemblies once; the definition loads and merges stylesheets once; window
settings are copied once when the native window is created. After that,
platform flags are simple runtime checks and permission calls are cached or
deduplicated, so the package adds no per-frame work to the render loop.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Attribute + reflection discoveryZero configuration, but trimming or aggressive AOT can remove the root type or its constructor; keep the root type rooted.
One root per applicationSimple entry points, but multi-window or multi-root apps need their own host layer.
Public parameterless constructorCacheable construction, but no constructor injection or DI lifetime model.
Stylesheet loading during discoveryAvoids per-frame reflection, but scans loaded assemblies and reads resources at startup.
Global static permission providerEasy app API, but process-wide; replacing it affects every consumer at once.
Mutable settings structAllocation-free composition, but default has surprising sentinel behaviour.
Host-agnostic enums in HostingAvoids implementation references in settings, at the cost of slightly surprising namespaces.
Legacy app contract retainedKeeps older projects compiling, but there are now two discovery paths to understand.

sections.title: Code tour
sections.text:
FileRead it for…
Hosting/Source/AppRootAttribute.csEvery root setting and the conversion to WindowSettings.
Hosting/Source/AppRootLocator.csEntry-assembly-first discovery, validation and legacy fallback.
Hosting/Source/AppRootDefinition.csThe object every host consumes: type, settings, styles and root factory.
Hosting/Source/WindowSettings.csNative window fields, defaults, sentinels and creation-time semantics.
Hosting/Source/AppModel.csThe legacy IDonkehApp/DonkehApp contract.
Hosting/Source/Host.csPlatform predicates and permission-provider installation.
Hosting/Source/HostPermissions.csGrant caching, in-flight deduplication and failure policy.

The mental model: Hosting is the layer that lets a host and an app agree on
what an application is. The app declares a root and settings; Hosting
discovers them, loads its styles, and hands a platform-neutral definition to
whichever native or browser host is running.

examples.label: App.cs

topics.title: Inspector
topics.summary:
Donkeh.Inspector is the in-app devtools panel. It is not a
separate viewer and it does not clone the application tree: it renders a
normal UILab component over the live mounted nodes, uses the same compiled
stylesheet and the same layout result, and queues every edit back to the
frame thread that owns the app.

sections.title: Three pieces
sections.text:
PieceRole
DevToolsStateShared mutable state: visibility, dock, tabs, selection, hover, expanded nodes, stylesheet table, layout result, performance samples and the deploy service.
InspectorPanelA normal Component that renders the toolbar, tree, styles, animations, performance and deploy tabs from that state.
DeployState / DownloadServerProject discovery, build targets, process execution, logs and the local HTTP download endpoint.
The window owns one DevToolsState and gives the panel its own
Renderer, LayoutEngine, renderer context and
display list. A docked panel reserves space from the app viewport; a
standalone panel runs in its own native window on a separate thread and
queues edits back to the frame thread.
The panel is a normal component
It uses the same builders, props, hooks and layout engine as the app. That
keeps the inspector honest: bugs in the panel are bugs in the engine. It also
means the inspector cannot use inline styles; state-dependent sizing is
encoded in generated utility classes.

sections.title: Shared state and refresh
sections.text:
The host updates DevToolsState from the frame loop and bumps a
single version counter. InspectorPanel.Tick() polls that version
and schedules a render only when it changed, so an idle inspector costs
almost nothing. Selection, hover and expansion use node identity
(ReferenceEqualityComparer), because nodes do not define value
equality.
Stylesheet and DOM mutations never run directly from the panel. They are
queued through QueueEdit and drained by the host before layout.
That is essential in window mode: the panel thread and the render thread are
different, and the table and box tree are not thread-safe.

sections.title: Elements tab
sections.text:
The tree is the logical tree, not just the live DOM shape. It includes
component and provider rows with their rendered output nested underneath, so
a developer can see why an element exists. Fragment nodes are followed
through; on first open the tree expands down to the first branching point,
at most eight levels.
FeatureBehaviour
Selection / hoverNode identity, with a highlight overlay drawn by the host over the selected box.
Inspect modePointer clicks pick the app element under the cursor instead of interacting with the app.
ExpansionA set of expanded nodes pruned every render when nodes unmount; selection can scroll itself into view.
Component rowsShow the component type and its current output kind without pretending to be an element.
Text rowsShow the text content and its node identity.
The Styles pane matches rules with the same DataTable and
RendererContext the app used, groups them by origin and selector,
and reverses the list so the strongest group is first. Rule ranges recorded
at stylesheet rebuild time label each match as user-agent,
author #N or devtools.
Computed values come from the real LayoutResult, not from a
second style pass. If the element has no box, the pane says so instead of
inventing values. The grouping is cached by element identity, element
revision, state version and table instance, because matching, selector text
and declaration interning are the expensive parts of the pane.
Editing
Declarations are edited in place. Property changes commit on Enter or focus
loss; value changes commit live when the text looks complete and again on
change. Pasting into the add row parses one or more declarations, or a whole
rule block, and applies them to the same group. Edits are queued as table
mutations, so the next app layout sees them through the normal cascade.
The inspector can also create an element-level style rule for the selected
node and add declarations to it. It does not restructure the application
tree. Its own highlight and selection markers are private
data-* attributes on the live elements, not a second app tree.

sections.title: Colour picker
sections.text:
ColorPreview converts between CSS colour text and the engine’s
packed 0xAARRGGBB. It understands #rgb,
#rgba, #rrggbb, #rrggbbaa,
comma/space/slash rgb()/rgba() and a small named
set. Unsupported syntax never throws; it simply does not get a swatch.
The picker is a modal popup with a 110 px hue/saturation wheel, a live hex
field and preset swatches. Pointer angle selects hue, distance selects
saturation, and value stays at full brightness. Every move queues a rule
value edit, but identical interned values are skipped. Preset rows are laid
out eight per row because the engine has no inline styles.

sections.title: Performance tab
sections.text:
The host samples frame, layout, render and UILab update timings, frame count,
instruction count, box count, node count, CPU, managed/working/private
memory, thread count and GC generations. Sampling is throttled: the window
updates roughly four times per second, and the panel refreshes about once per
second while this tab is active.
SurfaceContent
CardsFPS, CPU, managed/working set, GC counts, layout, render, update and total frames.
GraphsFrame history at a 33 ms scale, layout and render history at 16 ms scales.
BarsQuantised to 120 height classes; no inline styles or canvas drawing.
HistoryFixed-size ring buffers; the panel reads spans, it does not sample on the UI thread.

sections.title: Animations tab
sections.text:
Keyframes are read directly from the DataTable. Frames are
grouped by animation name in first-seen order, then stops are grouped by
selector text such as from, 50% or to.
Declarations are displayed from interned property and value ids. The selected
animation is part of DevToolsState; unknown selections fall back
to the first group.

sections.title: Deploy tab
sections.text:
DeployState discovers the application project, derives targets
from its target frameworks and provides build buttons plus logs. Discovery
starts beside the entry assembly, then the base and current directories, and
walks upward. A project whose name matches the entry assembly wins when a
folder contains several projects.
TargetCommand / output
Desktopdotnet build -c Release -f <tfm> -o builds/desktop
Androiddotnet build with APK packaging, then copy the signed APK to builds/android.
WebAssemblydotnet publish -f net10.0-browser -o builds/wasm, then verify index.html.
CustomA DeployTarget delegate receives project paths, output directory, configuration and a log sink.
Builds run on a worker and are sequential, because concurrent
dotnet build processes share intermediate directories. A busy
flag rejects overlapping starts; every target reports its own state, error,
duration, timestamp and trimmed log. Build output notifications are
throttled to a 200 ms window so a noisy build cannot monopolise the frame
loop.
Download server
The Deploy tab can expose the build directory over a tiny HTTP server. It
uses a raw TcpListener instead of HttpListener, so
no Windows URL reservation or administrator rights are needed. It binds all
IPv4 interfaces, supports GET, HEAD and a
POST /upload endpoint, lists the build directory, streams large
files, rejects path traversal and closes each connection after one request.
Uploads accept raw image bodies up to 32 MB, restrict the extension to known
image types and write into {project}/debug; the generated index
page exposes the drop area and posts one file per request.
Local-network file server, no authentication
The download server is intended for a trusted local network. Anyone who can
reach the port can browse and download the build artifacts and upload images
into the project's debug folder. Stop it when not deploying;
changing the root stops a running server.

sections.title: Host integration
sections.text:
The host compiles the inspector stylesheet after the user agent and author
sheets, so its rules win source-order ties. Dock sizes are generated as
dt-dockh-N and dt-dockw-N classes rather than
inline styles. DevToolsDock.Window opens a separate native
window on an STA thread and shares the same state; edits are queued and
drained on the app frame thread.
Hiding the inspector exits inspect mode, closes the colour picker and removes
the docked viewport reservation. Disabling devtools removes its shortcut and
skips its stylesheet, layout engine and overlay submission entirely.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Live tree, no cloneEdits and selection reflect the real app immediately, but the inspector must respect node lifetimes and thread ownership.
Panel is a UILab componentDogfoods the engine and reuses all layout/paint code, but every inspector layout costs a second engine pass.
Generated utility classesWorks without inline styles, but dock sizes and graph heights require a finite class table.
Heuristic project discoveryZero configuration for normal apps; a published app with no project files simply shows an empty Deploy tab.
Sequential buildsAvoids MSBuild directory races, at the cost of build-all latency.
Raw TCP download serverNo elevation or URL reservations, but no TLS, authentication or HTTP/1.1 keep-alive.
Throttled samplingKeeps the inspector cheap, but the graphs are a coarse diagnostic view, not a profiler trace.
Desktop-orientedWindow, docking and local build/deploy features assume the native host; the browser host does not include this inspector.

sections.title: Code tour
sections.text:
FileRead it for…

InspectorPanel.csToolbar, tree, styles grouping and editing, colour picker, animations, performance dashboard and deploy UI.

The mental model: the inspector is a second UILab application that observes
the first one through shared state. It can read the live tree, compiled table
and layout result cheaply, but it never owns them; edits go back through the
host’s queue so the real application remains the source of truth.

topics.title: LayoutLab
topics.summary:
LayoutLab is the largest package and the one with the widest
job: take a matched CSS table, resolve styles, generate boxes, run the
formatting contexts, measure text, evaluate animations, and emit a compact
paint-instruction stream. It is not a browser engine clone; it is a
deliberate approximation that covers the CSS a real application uses and
keeps the frame path predictable.

sections.title: The frame pipeline
sections.text:
One engine instance is reused across frames. A full layout pass is a
sequence of well-defined phases, not a recursive box routine hidden in a
renderer:
Layout(root, options)
├── frame setup          viewport, fonts, renderer context, signatures
├── style caches         resolve or reuse ComputedStyle per node
├── BuildBox             element boxes, anonymous text, ::before/::after
├── prune                drop cache entries for detached nodes
├── LayoutRootBox        block / inline / flex / grid / table / floats
├── ProcessAbsoluteBoxes absolute and fixed boxes, static positions
├── BuildDisplayList     stacking contexts, paint ops, scroll translations
└── Optimiser.Run        cull, merge, collapse scopes, compact constants
└── LayoutResult (boxes, instructions, constants)
The engine keeps the box tree in unscrolled absolute coordinates. Scroll
offsets are clamped per scroll container and applied as paint-time
translations. Scrolling can therefore repaint without rebuilding geometry,
and a viewport resize invalidates only the parts whose styles or metrics
actually depend on the new environment.

sections.title: Style resolution
sections.text:
StyleResolver receives the node, the parent’s computed style
and the already-ordered matched rules from Donkeh.Data. It
applies declarations weakest-first and runs important declarations in a
second pass, which lets !important win without allocating a
per-property cascade map.
- Inherited scalars  -  colour, font, writing mode and similar  -  are copied from the parent. Custom properties stay linked through StyleParent and are resolved lazily.
- Text nodes are forced to display: inline and fragments to display: contents; these are framework constructs, not authored CSS.
- Percentages, em, rem, viewport units and auto stay as CssLength values. Layout resolves them later against the correct containing block.
- Parsed declaration values are cached by interned value id in StyleValueCache, so repeated 0 8px values parse once.
ComputedStyle is a large mutable object rather than a frozen
record. That is deliberate: the animation runtime writes interpolated
values into the style between frames and reuses the same instance. Arrays,
filters and animation lists referenced by a style are treated as immutable
once published.

sections.title: Caches and invalidation
sections.text:
LayoutLab is built around the assumption that most of a frame does not
change. Several caches sit between the DOM and the geometry:
CacheKey / invalidationWhat it saves
Style cacheNode revision, parent inherited-value hash, frame signature, renderer-context version, interaction version.Re-cascading unchanged subtrees.
Inherited-value hashMemoised per ComputedStyle instance for the current pass.Recomputing whether a child inherited something different.
Value cacheInterned declaration value id.Parsing the same CSS value over and over.
Text layout cacheText, text style and quantised available width; two generations of up to 1024 entries.Re-wrapping and re-measuring identical runs.
Box cacheNode identity, optional and explicit.Allocating the box tree and child lists every frame.
Animation stateNode identity and a monotonic frame stamp.Restarting clocks and tracks for live nodes.
The style signature includes viewport, font metrics, orientation, device
pixel ratio and renderer context. Interaction state is a separate version,
because hover or focus on one node can change a sibling through a selector
without changing either node’s DOM revision. Height-only resizes are
special-cased: they do not invalidate width-based queries unless the table
contains height media queries or a style uses viewport-height units.
Results can alias engine storage
With SnapshotResults enabled the instruction stream and node
map are copied into the result. The box tree is still owned by the engine
and may be mutated in place when ReuseLayoutBoxes is enabled.
Treat a result as read-only, and snapshot it when it must outlive the next
frame.

sections.title: Box generation
sections.text:
BuildBox walks the DOM once. It creates a box for every
generated element, skips display: none, flattens
display: contents into its children, creates synthetic text
nodes for direct text in flex/grid containers, and materialises generated
::before/::after content from the CSS table. The
resulting LayoutBox carries the node, style, parent, children,
border/padding/content rectangles, margins, scroll metrics and float context.
Boxes are the unit of layout reuse. With reuse enabled, a cached box is
reset  -  geometry, children, text, scroll and float state  -  while its node
identity and child-list capacity are kept. That removes the per-frame
allocation of the entire tree at the cost of mutating the previous result.

sections.title: Formatting contexts
sections.text:
LayoutContent dispatches on the box’s formatting context. The
implementations share intrinsic-size measurement, length resolution,
floats and caching, so a nested flex item inside a grid cell inside a table
cell still behaves consistently.
ContextCoverage
Block and inline flowBlock flow, inline runs, line boxes, text wrapping, inline-blocks, floats and block formatting contexts.
FlexRow/column, reverse axes, wrapping, grow/shrink, basis, gaps, auto margins, order, justify and align, multi-line cross sizing.
GridExplicit tracks, fr, minmax(), auto-fit/auto-fill, named areas, row/column placement, spans, gaps and intrinsic contributions.
TableRow/cell collection, colspan/rowspan, max-content column sizing, collapsed or separate borders, border spacing and row-height refinement.
FloatsFloat context with clearance, avoidance by BFC roots and inline content flowing around active floats.
Out of flowAbsolute and fixed boxes deferred until normal flow finishes; static positions seeded before flex/grid/table skip them.
Flex is a good example of the engineering style. It rents scratch arrays
from ArrayPool<T>, sorts by order, calculates
base and minimum sizes, wraps lines, distributes positive and negative free
space, and runs up to four extra shrink passes to remove clamping overflow.
Auto minimum sizes use measured max-content as a floor, which is what keeps
a busy toolbar from crushing its buttons.
Grid uses a flattened track model (Fixed, Percent,
Fr, Auto, MinContent,
MaxContent, FitContent) and handles column flow by
transposing placement, line names and named areas. Table layout is
intentionally simpler: max-content column sizing with spanning-cell
distribution, then a second cell layout with final row heights.

sections.title: Text and line layout
sections.text:
Text is deliberately decoupled from fonts. ITextMeasurer reports
advance width, ascent and descent for a run; the default
SimpleTextMeasurer uses a deterministic per-character advance
table rather than font files. The window host can replace it with a
font-backed measurer without changing layout code.
TextLayoutEngine performs line breaking, whitespace handling,
alignment, direction, letter spacing, text transforms and decoration
metadata. The result is a TextLayout of positioned lines, cached
by text, style and quantised width. Because the cache is bounded to two
generations, a live performance monitor or other constantly changing text
can disable text caching without affecting style resolution.
Approximation is a feature
Simple metrics make layout deterministic and cheap, and they keep the
engine independent of platform font stacks. The visible renderer still
measures real glyphs when it draws; LayoutLab only needs consistent advance
widths to decide line boxes.

sections.title: Paint instructions
sections.text:
Layout does not call OpenGL. It emits a portable display list. Each
Instruction is a fixed 24-byte value: four floats, an opcode,
flags, a 16-bit auxiliary index and a 32-bit payload. Small draws use the
floats directly; text, gradients, borders, transforms and other large
payloads live in a ConstantPool and are addressed by index.
Paint stageWhat it emits
BackgroundColour, gradients, background images, layers, clipping and repeat.
Borders and outlinesPer-side borders, rounded corners, collapsed table edges, outline offsets and triangle borders.
Shadows and effectsOuter and inset shadows, filters, backdrop filters, blend modes and opacity scopes.
TextLine runs, decoration, selection/caret overlays and placeholder colours.
Replaced contentImages, video frames and other host-supplied content.
ScrollbarsHost-painted scrollbar tracks and thumbs derived from scroll metrics.
The display-list builder walks stacking contexts in paint order, defers
fixed boxes to a second pass with inherited opacity, and applies scroll
translations while emitting. Transform, opacity, filter, clip-path, mask,
blend and composited-layer pushes are represented as explicit scoped
instructions so the renderer can batch and the optimiser can reason about
them.

sections.title: The optimiser
sections.text:
Optimiser.Run is a small, semantics-preserving pass over the
instruction stream. It drops no-op instructions and optional frame markers,
intersects clips, removes empty or redundant clips, drops identity opacity
scopes, culls draws outside the active clip when no transform or filter is
active, merges adjacent opaque rectangles, and optionally compacts the
constant pool. Rounded clips are never treated as redundant, and unmatched
pops are ignored rather than truncating the frame.

sections.title: Animations and transitions
sections.text:
AnimationRuntime is frame-driven and owns all per-node timing
state. The host supplies a monotonic time through
LayoutOptions.AnimationTimeSeconds; the runtime never reads the
wall clock. Keyframe tracks are parsed lazily from the DataTable
and cached by interned animation name. Transitions and keyframes share the
same interpolation model: supported properties interpolate, discrete
properties switch at the segment midpoint, and unsupported values keep their
base style.
The runtime distinguishes paint-only animations from layout animations.
Transform and opacity changes can refresh the display list without a full
layout pass; width, height, margin and similar changes cannot. A per-frame
stamp lets Prune drop state for nodes that left the tree, which
prevents unmounted panels and removed carousel slides from staying alive
through their animation state.

sections.title: Repaint without relayout
sections.text:
Repaint rebuilds the display list from an existing box tree
when geometry is still valid. Scroll offsets never move boxes, so scrolling
refreshes scroll metrics and re-emits instructions without re-resolving
styles. RepaintAnimated is the same idea for paint-only
animations. This split is the main reason a scrolled or hovered UI does not
pay for a full style and layout pass.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Approximate text metrics by defaultLayout widths are deterministic but not pixel-identical to the final font rasteriser. A host can plug in real metrics.
CSS subset, not a browser cloneSome advanced layout modes, generated-content functions and font features are approximated or unsupported.
Mutable computed stylesAnimation can write in place, but sharing a style across threads or assuming immutability is unsafe.
Box reuse mutates resultsFast, but a LayoutResult is only stable when snapshotted and never mutated by the next frame.
Single layout threadNo locking in the hot path, but the engine, caches and animation runtime cannot be driven concurrently.
Depth capMaxLayoutDepth defaults to 512; nodes at the limit receive a box but their children are not visited.
Table layout is simplifiedMax-content column sizing and equal extra-space distribution, not the full CSS table algorithm.
Display list is a contractThe renderer must respect scoped opcodes and the constant-pool layout; changing opcode semantics is a cross-package change.

The useful way to read LayoutLab is as a pipeline of representations:
matched rules → computed styles → boxes → geometry → paint instructions.
Each stage caches what it can, invalidates narrowly, and hands the next
stage a compact value-oriented shape rather than a tree of rich objects.

topics.title: Parser
topics.summary:
The CSS parser is a single-pass lexer wrapped around a declaratively
registered exact-match engine. The outer scan stays hand-written and
allocation-conscious; the keyword, property, function and pseudo-selector
tables are compiled into specialised IL once, on first use.

sections.title: The design goal
sections.text:
The target was an unusual combination: the authoring ergonomics of a
rule-based tokenizer with the execution profile of hand-written code. Rule
engines usually pay for their flexibility with intermediate representations,
dictionary probes, virtual dispatch or an interpreter in the hot loop. None
of those are acceptable when a stylesheet is re-tokenized often enough to
show up in frame time.
The split that made it work is simple. The declaration of lexical
knowledge is separate from its execution. Rules are registered
through small helpers, then a runtime IL compiler turns that registration
table into a dense first-character dispatch table and one specialised
matcher per first character. After type initialisation there is no rule
interpreter, no name lookup and no general-purpose matching engine between
the input span and the generated code.
It is a runtime compiler, not a build-time source generator
The generated code is emitted with System.Reflection.Emit from
the tokenizer's static constructor. The rule definitions themselves are
ordinary C# registration calls in Rules/*.cs,
Tokenizer/PseudoClasses.cs, PseudoElements.cs and
Functions/*.cs. A future build-time generator could bake the
same matcher into the assembly, but the current implementation trades a
small first-touch cost for a tiny, declarative source surface.

sections.title: Two layers, one pass
sections.text:
Tokenizer.Parse runs a hand-written switch over the current
character. That outer loop owns everything structural: whitespace, comments,
strings, numbers, dimensions, hashes, at-keywords, punctuation, escapes,
CDO/CDC and the declaration-colon disambiguation. It emits at most one token
per iteration.
Names are the only place where the lexer needs a large table of lexical
knowledge. Once ScanName has consumed a maximal identifier, the
exact matcher decides whether it is a property name, a function name, a
pseudo-class, a pseudo-element or just an identifier. That boundary is
deliberate: the hot structural scan stays obvious and debuggable, while the
large, repetitive keyword table is generated.
Tokenizer.Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>)
└── hand-written scan
├── whitespace / comments / CDO / CDC
├── strings, escapes, numbers, dimensions, percentages
├── punctuation and combinators
└── ScanName(...)
└── ClassifyName(...)
├── '(' lookahead  → Function
├── MinLengthByFirstChar early-out
└── ExactMatch(ReadOnlySpan<char>)   // generated IL
└── first-character group → length switch → trie

sections.title: The declarative rule set
sections.text:
RuleBuilder exposes the authoring API:
Exact, CssPropertyName,
CssPropertyGroup, CssPseudoClass,
CssPseudoElement and Function. The per-letter
PropertiesA() through PropertiesZ() methods are
just registration calls, grouped so the source stays auditable and diff
friendly.
The current table contains 795 exact rules:
Rule kindCountExample
CSS property names577grid-template-columns
Functions100clamp, linear-gradient
Pseudo-classes78:focus-visible
Pseudo-elements30::placeholder
Punctuation rules10:;(){}[]>
The 577 property names demonstrate why the table is generated rather than
hand-coded. The layout engine only implements a subset (168 registered
properties today), but the tokenizer still recognises the wider CSS
vocabulary so later stages can make the policy decision. A name being
tokenized as a property does not mean its value grammar is fully supported.
Duplicate kinds are resolved deliberately
A name can be both a property and a function, such as color,
rotate or scale. RuleBuilder.Exact
lets the property registration win, and ClassifyName upgrades
the token to TokenKind.Function when the next character is
(. The lexer never has to guess from the name alone.

code.label: RuleBuilder

sections.title: Compiling the matcher
sections.text:
The static constructor in Rules/Rules.cs registers every rule,
computes a 65,536-entry MinLengthByFirstChar table, and calls
Compiler.CompileExactRules. Compilation groups the rules by
first character and emits one DynamicMethod per group.
Compiled shapeValue
Distinct first-character groups34
Single-rule groups (skip the length switch)11
Multi-rule groups23
Largest group110 rules, starting with :
Shortest / longest rule text1 / 39 characters
The public entry point is a dense array of delegates plus the lowest first
character covered by the table. An empty span or an out-of-range first
character returns -1 without calling generated code:
Inside a group, generated IL switches on exact length first. This
is the key to longest-match behaviour and to killing prefix ambiguity:
border and border-radius are different rules with
different lengths, so a six-character candidate can never fall through to a
shorter rule. The lexer already scanned the maximal identifier, so the
matcher receives the complete candidate rather than a prefix.
The trie only splits when a node still has more than six candidates. Below
that threshold, a linear chain of
MemoryExtensions.SequenceEqual<char> calls is smaller and
often faster than another switch. Single-rule groups skip the length switch
entirely, which keeps punctuation buckets tiny. The compiler also emits
longer buckets before shorter ones so the generated method layout favours
the more specific rules.
Why one method per first character?
The compiler comments call out a measurable JIT cliff: a single matcher of
roughly 20 KB was slower than a table of small methods. Splitting by first
character keeps each generated method below the large-method optimisation
threshold, gives the JIT a simple constant range for its switch tables, and
makes the hot path a predictable array index plus a short delegate call.

code.label: CompiledExactMatcher.Match
Generated matcher shape

sections.title: What the hot path actually does
sections.text:
For a property-heavy stylesheet, most name classification follows this
sequence:
- ScanName walks the maximal identifier, handling escapes and non-ASCII characters without allocating.
- ClassifyName checks whether the next character is (. If so, the token is a function and the exact table is skipped entirely.
- MinLengthByFirstChar[first] rejects candidates shorter than any rule with that first character. Single-letter identifiers never enter the generated matcher.
- ExactMatch indexes the first-character group, switches on length and walks a small character trie or comparison chain.
- The result is written into Token as a packed (start, length) location plus an interned text id.
The submitted character stream is never sliced into temporary strings. A
token stores only the interned id and a 32-bit location: 24 bits of start
offset and 8 bits of length. A Token is 12 bytes, so a
megabyte-scale stylesheet with roughly 380,000 tokens uses about 4.6 MB for
the token buffer before list overhead.
The 255-character and 16.7-million-character limits are real
The packed location cannot address a source longer than 16,777,215
characters. Tokens longer than 255 characters, such as a large
data: URI or string, are split into consecutive chunks that
share a kind; downstream consumers concatenate chunk text to recover the
original value.

sections.title: Allocation behaviour
sections.text:
The tokenizer consumes ReadOnlySpan<char> and advances by
index; it does not materialise an intermediate token-text array. The token
destination is a List<Token> written through
CollectionsMarshal.AsSpan, so the loop avoids
List<Token>.Add and its bounds/count bookkeeping.
MechanismWhat it buys
ReadOnlySpan<char> + indicesNo substring allocation for scanning, matching or token boundaries.
Packed Token.Location12-byte tokens instead of separate start/end integers.
Pre-sized token bufferInitial capacity is max(16, sourceLength / 2 + 16); the benchmark corpus needs no growth.
CollectionsMarshal.SetCountWrites directly into the backing array and trims to the exact count once at the end.
Interned textRepeated names and punctuation become stable integer ids used by later stages.
The honest caveat is that “zero allocation” describes the steady state, not
the first time a document introduces a new token text. InternTable
allocates the string on first sighting, then stores it in a dense global
table. Subsequent lookups use a thread-static front cache and
AlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>>, so the common
case does not need a lock or a new string. Single ASCII punctuation
characters use a pre-computed 128-entry id table, which removes the global
lock from the most frequent tokens in CSS.
The table never evicts. Its size follows the number of distinct token texts,
not the number of tokens, which is the right trade-off for finite
stylesheets but something to keep in mind for long-running apps that
generate unbounded CSS text. Reusing a cleared token list avoids the one
large backing-array allocation per document.

sections.title: Performance
sections.text:
The parser benchmark has two measurements: the exact matcher over a hot
token stream, and a full Tokenizer.Parse over a synthetic
stylesheet built from every registered rule. The quick runner uses warmup
plus repeated runs, and reports the best run.
MeasurementResult
Corpus1,013,028 bytes, 381,640 tokens
Full parse time4.97 ms per document
Document throughput203.8 MB/s
Token throughput76.8 M tokens/s
Steady-state allocation0 B per parse
Exact matcher4.81 ns/token, 207.9 M tokens/s
Matcher text throughput1,926.4 MB/s
Matcher allocation0 B per pass
IL compilation0.98 ms, 484,952 B, 0 GC collections
These numbers were measured on .NET 10.0.10, Windows 10, a 12-logical-core
workstation with workstation GC in interactive latency mode. They are a
shape, not a promise: token distribution, CPU, GC mode and whether the
intern table is warm all move the result. The important part is the ratio
between full-document throughput and raw matcher throughput: the structural
scan and token writing dominate, while keyword classification is already in
the low-single-digit-nanoseconds-per-token range.
Why the compiler cost is acceptable
Compilation is a one-time type-initialisation cost, not a per-document cost.
The quick benchmark measures roughly a millisecond and half a megabyte for
the IL pass after the rules are registered. In a desktop app this happens
once before the first stylesheet is parsed; the alternative is interpreting
a 795-rule table on every token.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost or limitation
Runtime IL instead of a build-time artifactAdds a small first-touch cost and depends on DynamicMethod. A build-time generator would remove both and be friendlier to ahead-of-time publishing.
One generated method per first characterMore methods and delegates to manage, but each method stays below the JIT large-method threshold.
Exact matching, not prefix matchingRequires the scanner to consume the maximal identifier first. That is exactly what makes longest-match correct and keeps the generated trie small.
Linear comparison below six candidatesDeliberately trades a few comparisons for smaller code and better instruction-cache behaviour.
Global interningIds are stable for the process but the table grows forever; it is not a cache with eviction.
Packed token locationExcellent density, but a 16.7M-character source limit and 255-character token chunks are visible constraints.
Hand-written structural lexerSome CSS context is resolved with look-behind, for example distinguishing a declaration colon from a pseudo-class colon after a property name.
One deliberately non-obvious case is background-position:right
with no whitespace after the colon. A context-free lexer would see
:right as a pseudo-class. IsDeclarationColon checks
whether the previous token is a property name preceded by { or
;, and emits a plain colon instead. Selectors keep their
pseudo-class token because their preceding tokens do not match that shape.

sections.text:

The useful mental model is: the scanner decides where a token ends,
and the generated matcher decides what a maximal name means. Keeping
those responsibilities separate is what allows the declarative rule table to
be large without putting an interpreter in the per-character path.

topics.title: UILab
topics.summary:
UILab is the component layer: a small React-shaped runtime
for C#. It owns the virtual tree, component instances, hooks, context,
routing and the reconciliation that turns a new render into in-place
mutations of the live tree. That live tree is also the DOM the CSS matcher
and layout engine consume, so there is no second translation step between
the component model and the engine.

sections.title: One tree, two roles
sections.text:
Every node implements IgniteSupportedDomNode. The same tree
that describes elements and text is the tree the selector matcher walks and
the layout engine boxes. UILab does not render pixels; it produces a live
DOM-shaped tree and a version number that tells the host when to repaint.
Component.Render()
└── Node description
├── ElementNode      real element, attributes, events, children
├── TextNode         text run
├── FragmentNode     transparent grouping
├── ComponentNode    logical: instance + last output
└── ProviderNode     logical: context value + child scope
│
└── Renderer mount / diff
└── live tree (elements, text, fragments)
├── Donkeh.Data selector matching
└── Donkeh.LayoutLab boxes and paint
Component and provider nodes never appear in the live tree. They stay in
the virtual tree so their instances and published context values survive
across renders. The host only ever sees the materialised output.

sections.title: Building a tree
sections.text:
_ is the terse builder: H for elements,
Text for text, C<T> for components,
F for fragments and helpers such as Show and
Each. HtmlHelper adds 138 typed element factories
that produce exactly the same nodes, so Div(...) and
H("div", ...) are interchangeable.
Element attributes and class names are interned immediately. A
Props value is converted into an id-based representation once,
so the diff compares integers rather than strings. Dedicated properties
such as Id, ClassName, Href and
Disabled are applied before the arbitrary
Attributes dictionary; a class entry appends
tokens, while an id entry replaces the dedicated id.
Text children are first-class. A pure-text child list is folded into the
element’s TextContent instead of allocating one
TextNode per run, which is a significant win for labels,
buttons and table cells. Numeric and boolean values obtain implicit text
conversions using invariant culture so rendered numbers stay stable across
machines.

code.label: Builders

sections.title: Components and lifecycle
sections.text:
A component is a class with a public parameterless constructor and a
Render method. The renderer creates exactly one instance per
mounted ComponentNode, assigns props and context scope, and
reuses the instance for every later render. Unmounting discards it, which is
exactly why hook state lives as long as the component stays in the tree.
MemberWhen it runs
Render()During mount and every update. Hooks are only legal inside this window.
OnMount()After the first subtree commit and ref attachment, before the root mount returns.
OnUpdate()After a committed re-render. Not called when ShouldRender vetoes a parent-driven render.
OnUnmount()Before hook cleanups and before the mounted flag is cleared.
ShouldRender()Lets a component skip a parent-driven render while still receiving new props and context.
Component<TProps> adds a typed Props
payload. Props are assigned before ShouldRender, so an override
can compare old and new values. A null render result is a bug,
not an empty view; return an empty fragment instead.

sections.title: Reconciliation
sections.text:
The renderer mounts an initial tree and then diffs every later render in
place. It never rebuilds the whole tree. Nodes keep their identity, and
mutations bump revisions only when something actually changed, which is what
preserves layout cache entries for untouched subtrees.
StepBehaviour
Kind checkComponents match by exact type, providers by Context<T> identity, elements by interned tag name, fragments and text by kind.
MismatchUnmount the old subtree and mount the new one, discarding component state below it.
Element matchPatchFrom rewrites attributes, classes, events and refs in place; children are diffed recursively.
Text matchThe existing TextNode is reused; assigning identical text suppresses the revision bump.
Keyed childrenMatched by key regardless of position, so reorders move nodes instead of remounting them.
Unkeyed childrenTry the same index first, then the first unused positional slot of the same kind.
Unused old childrenUnmounted after the new list is built, releasing refs, handlers and component state.
A component whose output is another component or provider has no live node
of its own. The renderer pushes the parent output slot down the logical chain
until it reaches the first live node, which lets a nested component replace
itself in place when its output kind changes.

sections.title: Hooks
sections.text:
Hook identity is positional. Each component owns an append-only list of hook
slots, and BeginRender resets a cursor to zero. The nth hook
call always maps to the nth slot; adding, removing or moving a hook changes
the sequence and throws instead of silently corrupting state.
HookStorage and behaviour
State / StateWithUpdateValue plus a stable setter; equality suppresses unchanged writes. Functional updates read the current value at call time.
ReducerState plus a stable dispatcher. The latest reducer is captured each render; unchanged results do not queue work.
Effect / LayoutEffectDependency arrays compared element by element. Cleanup runs before the next body and on unmount; layout effects run before passive effects.
Memo / CallbackCaches a value or delegate by dependency array; without dependencies the factory runs every render.
UseRefStable mutable box. Writes never schedule a render; element refs are attached on mount and cleared on unmount.
UseContextReads the nearest provider from the scope captured at render time, falling back to the context’s default.
State setters throw during render. That is intentional: a render must be a
pure function of the captured state. Updates belong in event handlers or
effects, where they are queued and applied by the flush loop.

sections.title: The flush loop
sections.text:
State updates mark a component dirty and enqueue it once. With
AutoFlush on, the queue flushes synchronously; with it off, the
host calls Flush from its frame loop. The loop processes every
dirty component, commits effects, and repeats if an effect queued more work.
A hard limit of 64 passes catches an effect that updates state
unconditionally.
Effects run only after the whole dirty queue has been applied, so they
observe a fully patched tree rather than a half-updated one. Components are
visited in render order and hooks in declaration order. Version
is a wake-up counter, not a content hash: a flush that processes a component
bumps it even if the resulting tree is identical.

code.label: Flush loop

sections.title: Context
sections.text:
Context<T> is identified by instance identity, not by type.
A provider publishes a value into an immutable scope chain; consumers read
the nearest matching scope. Values are captured per render, so a later
state-driven render sees the same context it saw when it was rendered.
A provider republishing a different value does not by itself force existing
consumers to re-render; they update the next time they render for some other
reason. Providers render as transparent fragments, so context does not add a
box to the layout tree. Routing is built on the same mechanism:
AppRouter publishes Router.Path and
Router.SetPage.

sections.title: Events and refs
sections.text:
Events are ordinary delegates stored in an element’s event map keyed by a
normalised lowercase name. Props exposes simple handlers such as
OnClick, OnPointerDown, OnContextMenu,
OnInput and OnKeyDown, plus typed
On…Event variants such as OnClickEvent and
OnKeyDownEvent. Arbitrary events can go through
On(name, handler) or Attr(name, handler). Hosts mirror
handler presence into their own event system, but the delegate stays owned by
the element.
Every host dispatch is represented by an Event subclass, even
when the payload is empty. MouseEvent adds window and
element-local coordinates, KeyDownEvent exposes the key and its
modifiers, InputEvent and ChangeEvent carry the
control value, and the media classes carry playback time. Typed handlers take
precedence over the simple delegate for the same event name.
Pointer handlers receive element-local coordinates. A
ContextMenuEvent also exposes the deepest clicked node as
Target, the node whose handler is running as
CurrentTarget, and the original pointer position in window CSS
pixels. The complete event list lives in the
event reference.
Ref<ElementNode> points at a mounted element and is cleared
on unmount. Refs are an escape hatch for host integration and measurements,
not a way to drive rendering: writing to a ref never schedules work.

sections.title: Stylesheets and assets
sections.text:
[assembly: Stylesheet("path.css")] declares an embedded CSS
resource. Stylesheet.Load() scans assemblies and type/module
attributes, reads the matching embedded resources and concatenates them. It
is reflection-heavy and uncached, so load once at startup and keep the
string. Packed images use the parallel [Image] / Image
API.

sections.title: Why it stays cheap
sections.text:
- Interned identity. Tag names, attribute names, class names and attribute values are integer ids, so patches compare ints.
- In-place mutation. The live tree is reused; only changed fields bump revisions, preserving layout caches for untouched subtrees.
- Text folding. All-text children collapse into one TextContent string instead of allocating one node per run.
- One queue entry per component. Repeated state updates in one pass collapse through the Queued flag.
- Static component factories. Reflection for the public parameterless constructor happens once per component type, then a cached delegate is reused.
- Stable keyed matching. Reorders move existing nodes and preserve component state instead of remounting a list.
- No second tree translation. The live tree is already the DOM consumed by matching and layout.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
Positional hooksFast and allocation-light, but hooks must be unconditional and in stable order.
Mutable live nodesNo tree rebuild, but the tree is not thread-safe and must only be touched by its renderer.
Public parameterless constructorsSimple, cacheable construction, but components cannot receive constructor dependencies.
Per-render context snapshotsPredictable reads, but publishing a new value does not automatically notify every consumer.
No error boundariesA throwing render or effect bubbles to the host; there is no component-level recovery boundary.
Keyed matching by linear scanFine for typical lists; very large lists pay for the scan rather than maintaining an index.
Silent no-op after unmountA late state setter is harmless, which also means a missed cleanup may go unnoticed.
One renderer per treeMounted once, single-threaded, no concurrent rendering or SSR path.
