topics.title: Windowing
topics.summary:
Donkeh.Windowing is the native desktop host. It owns the
window loop, the OpenGL renderer, input and focus, text and font atlases,
image and media caches, scrollbars, the built-in inspector, and the desktop
entry point that turns an [AppRoot] into a running application.
It is the layer where the portable engine meets a real platform.

sections.title: Entry and lifetime
sections.text:
Desktop apps do not write a Main. The build targets generate one
that calls AppRootHost.RunDesktop(args). That helper discovers
the app root, creates a DonkehWindow from its settings, and runs
the root component and merged stylesheet. The host also understands
--screenshot <path>, which captures frame 120 and closes
the window for deterministic smoke tests.
AppRootHost.RunDesktop(args)
├── AppRootLocator.Find()
├── new DonkehWindow(app.Settings)  // compiles UA + inspector CSS
└── window.Run(app.CreateRoot(), app.Styles)
├── Silk.NET window / view creation
├── Load: GL, fonts, images, renderer, input
├── Render: flush → layout → paint → submit
└── Close: release GPU resources, dispose window
DonkehWindow can run either a Silk.NET desktop window or an
attached IView supplied by a platform host. That is the seam
the Android host uses: the same window, layout and renderer logic runs
against an externally owned surface instead of creating a desktop window.

sections.title: The frame loop
sections.text:
OnRender is a fixed sequence. The ordering matters because each
stage decides whether the next one can reuse work:
- Process pending pointer movement and pointer auto-scroll.
- Raise BeforeFrame, the earliest host hook.
- Advance smooth-scroll animations and sample the monotonic animation clock.
- Flush UILab (and the inspector's renderer), then drain inspector edits and sync audio/video elements.
- Read view size, framebuffer size and DPI; reserve space for a docked inspector.
- Full layout, animated-style repaint, or scroll-only repaint  -  whichever is needed.
- Prune interaction nodes, build overlays, submit the display lists and flush the renderer.
- Run batched canvas recordings, then raw GL canvas callbacks.
- Update inspector sampling and handle a pending screenshot.
The window distinguishes NeedsLayout, NeedsPaint
and NeedsAnimatedPaint. A UILab version change or a resize forces
layout; a scroll forces only the display list; a transform or opacity
animation refreshes styles and paint without rebuilding geometry. CSS
animations are re-laid-out at 60 Hz while presentation can stay at 144 Hz,
which bounds CPU cost without making motion look choppy.

sections.title: The OpenGL renderer
sections.text:
GLRenderer executes LayoutLab's instruction stream. It does not
issue one draw per element. Every paint instruction becomes a fixed-size
160-byte GpuInstance carrying its clip rectangle, affine
transform, colour, SDF parameters and texture selector. Shapes, text and
images all become instanced quads in one GPU-resident stream.
MechanismEffect
Per-instance clip and transformClip or transform changes do not split batches; they are fragment-shader inputs.
16 texture slotsUp to sixteen textures per batch; exceeding it starts a new texture epoch while preserving paint order.
Indirect pathOne indirect command per segment, submitted with multi-draw when available, otherwise draw-indirect.
Direct fallbackSame geometry, one instanced draw per batch, for drivers without indirect support or for benchmarking.
Three stream slotsPersistent mapped instance/command buffers rotate so the CPU can prepare frame N+1 while the GPU reads N.
Unified shaderRects, rounded rects, borders, ellipses, shadows, glyphs and images share one vertex expansion path.
Window maskRounded window corners are applied in the shader and mirrored into the native window region where supported.
The renderer owns the shader program, VAOs, instance and command buffers,
fallback white texture and gradient cache. FontManager and
ImageCache are borrowed and must outlive it. Every member must
run on the GL context thread.

sections.title: Text and fonts
sections.text:
FontManager is a compact TrueType pipeline shared by layout and
painting. It discovers system fonts, caches faces per normalised request and
builds a fallback chain per face set. Glyphs are rasterised into atlases per
rounded pixel size; metrics are cached per quarter CSS pixel. Because
TrueTypeTextMeasurer and the renderer use the same manager,
measured line widths and painted advances always agree.
Measurement adds glyph advances and letter spacing, kerns adjacent runes on
the same face, and selects fallback faces per rune while keeping ascent and
descent from the primary face for stable line boxes. There is no shaping,
bidi reordering or tab expansion. Font and glyph caches are never evicted;
they live until the GL context is disposed.
The native host accepts WOFF 1.0 and WOFF 2.0 files in addition to TTF and
OTF. Containers are expanded to sfnt bytes with the fully managed
Meziantou.Framework.Fonts decoder, so the same path works on
desktop and Android without a native FreeType build. The expanded bytes then
go through the existing StbTrueType face, metrics and atlas pipeline.
RegisterFont takes an optional weight and italic flag and wins
over system-font discovery for the same family. A single regular registration
also serves bold and italic requests when no matching style was registered.
Advanced hosts can expose the window's Fonts manager directly;
the browser host uses the browser's own font loading instead.
Author stylesheets are not limited to embedded files. Before compiling the
cascade, the native host expands @import URLs (HTTP, file and
data), fetches each @font-face source, caches it under the temp
directory and registers the family automatically. Imports are cycle-guarded
and relative URLs resolve against the declaring sheet. This is what lets a
CDN icon font load without a manual RegisterFont call.
Two CSS details matter for icon fonts. Simple :is(a, b) selector
lists in author CSS are expanded into comma-separated selectors because the
matcher deliberately rejects logical pseudo-classes. ::before
and ::after content strings decode CSS hexadecimal escapes such
as \f0c9, so icon codepoints resolve to real glyphs.
donkeh enable-feature hot-reload adds the separate
Donkeh.HotReload package to the Debug configuration. It maps
embedded declarations back to source files and polls them from the window's
frame loop. A change calls SetStylesheet, so the complete
table, both layout engines, style caches and the inspector's sheet ranges
are rebuilt exactly as a programmatic stylesheet change would. The same
package watches component source files; after the .NET Hot Reload agent
patches a method body it calls RefreshComponents, which marks
every mounted component dirty and lets the normal diff produce the new
output without remounting or resetting hook state. Release builds never
reference the package, so the watcher is not part of the application
output.

sections.title: Images, audio, video and canvas
sections.text:
These primitives all live at the host boundary because they need platform
resources the layout engine must not know about:
PrimitiveWindowing responsibility
imgResolve file/data/packed sources, decode intrinsic dimensions, upload textures, apply object-fit and share the cache with CSS backgrounds.
audioOwn the SoundFlow device and one player per element; playback setup runs on a worker, while controls and events are serviced on the frame thread.
videoOwn the LibVLC player, request 640×360 RGBA frames, copy the latest frame into a dynamic texture and paint host controls.
canvasRun OnDraw recordings inside the indirect batch and OnContext callbacks after the batch flush.
Audio and video players are created asynchronously and pruned when their
elements leave the tree. Audio publishes state only after construction
finishes; video keeps a CPU frame buffer and uploads only when a new frame
arrives. The same screenshot, media and canvas paths are unavailable or
different on the browser host, which mirrors the DOM instead of running this
GL pipeline.

sections.title: Input, focus and interaction
sections.text:
Input is resolved against the layout tree, not the DOM. A pointer hit walks
the box tree, respects pointer-events, scroll containers and
fixed boxes, and updates a chain of hovered and active elements. Focus is a
separate chain with optional focus-visible state, caret placement and
selection.
InteractionImplementation
Hover / activeElement flags on the node chain; style caches use an interaction version so sibling and descendant selectors refresh.
Text editingFocused text controls own caret, selection, clipboard, IME composition and keyboard navigation.
Select menusHost-painted popup list positioned from the select box; hit testing and option selection are explicit overlays.
ScrollingWheel deltas find the nearest scroll container, clamp offsets, animate smooth scroll and repaint without relayout.
Touch panWith EnableTouchScrolling, a finger drag pans the nearest container that scrolls on the gesture's dominant axis; taps replay as clicks.
Context menuA right-button press bubbles to the nearest ancestor with an OnContextMenu handler. The event carries the deepest clicked node, the handling node and both window and element-local coordinates.
ScrollbarsHost-painted thumbs and tracks with drag interaction and pointer auto-scroll. Touch hosts get a wider grab area beside the bar.
Media controlsPlay/pause, scrubber and seek-drag handled directly by the window.
Frameless windowsapp-region: drag starts a native window drag; edge/corner hit testing provides resize handles.
CursorComputed cursor maps to a native standard cursor and is applied on the hover chain.
Context menus are opt-in per element. Attach the handler to a container to
treat a whole list as one menu area, then read e.Target to find
the row that was actually clicked:
H("div", new Props
{
OnContextMenu = e =>
{
var clicked = e.Target;          // deepest element under the pointer
var owner = e.CurrentTarget;     // element that owns this handler
Console.WriteLine($"menu at {e.WindowX},{e.WindowY}");
}
}, rows);
Android and desktop share the same right-button path. Desktop dispatches
the event on the right-button press. Android also treats a stationary
500 ms touch as a context-menu request; moving more than 10 px or starting
a drag/pan cancels it, and the release click is suppressed after it fires.
Scrolling is especially important to the frame budget. Box geometry stays in
unscrolled coordinates; scroll offsets are clamped per container and applied
as paint translations. A wheel event or scrollbar drag therefore rebuilds the
display list and hit-test offsets, but never the box tree or resolved styles.

sections.title: The inspector
sections.text:
The built-in inspector runs as a separate UILab tree with its own
Renderer, LayoutEngine, renderer context and
display list. When docked, it reduces the app viewport so the page reflows
instead of being covered. In window mode it runs in its own native window and
edits are queued back to the frame thread before layout.
Inspector work is throttled. The Performance tab samples roughly four times
per second rather than every frame; the Elements tab refreshes on UILab
version changes; selection scrolling is requested explicitly. Disabling
devtools removes its key handling and skips its stylesheet, layout engine and
overlay work entirely.

sections.title: DPI, sizing and window shape
sections.text:
The window works in CSS pixels and maps from the framebuffer using the
reported ratio, or an explicit DpiScale on platforms that report
physical surfaces. Pointer coordinates are divided by the same ratio, so hits
land on the CSS pixel layout used. Min/max client sizes are enforced by
nudging the native window back into range; resize events collapse into one
layout per rendered frame.
Frameless windows use the CSS app-region and host-provided
resize handles. A configured corner radius is applied both in the shader and,
where the platform supports it, to the native window region. The clear colour
is skipped for rounded windows so the corners can show the desktop while the
root element paints the visible surface.

sections.title: Trade-offs and sharp edges
sections.text:
DecisionCost
One frame threadNo locking in the hot path, but layout, rendering, input and media synchronisation must stay on that thread.
OpenGL-only native pathFast and portable across desktop/Android, but requires a GL context and has no software fallback.
Approximate text shapingFallback and kerning only; no complex shaping, bidi or tab layout.
Unbounded font/image cachesNo steady-state re-decoding, but memory grows with distinct fonts and image sources.
Fixed video frame size640×360 keeps uploads predictable, at the cost of resolution for large displays.
Optional input backendRendering survives a failed input platform, but the app is non-interactive until input works.
Separate inspector treeIsolation and independent layout, but duplicated renderers, style state and overlay submission.
Desktop-oriented hostAndroid reuses the window through an attached view; browser rendering is a different DOM host entirely.

description and a real GL surface. LayoutLab decides what to paint; Windowing
decides where the pixels go, what the pointer is over, which textures exist,
and how much of the previous frame can be reused.

tree the renderer draws and writes style edits back into the live
stylesheet.

topics.title: Using the animations tab

sections.title: Open the tab
sections.text:
Open the inspector, then choose Animations in the tab strip.
The tab reads the current compiled CSS table; it does not sample the live
animation clock.

sections.title: The two panes
sections.text:
- The left pane lists keyframe groups by name, in first-seen order.
- Click a group to inspect it.
- The right pane lists each stop, its declaration count and the property values.
- If the selected animation disappears, the inspector falls back safely and shows an empty selection.
- When no keyframes are registered, the tab shows a quiet placeholder instead of an empty list.

sections.title: Where the groups come from
sections.text:
Any @keyframes rule parsed from the built-in or author
stylesheets is collected. A typical component stylesheet looks like this:
The Animations tab groups the three stops under pulse. The
card in the right pane also shows the number of declarations so a missing
property is easy to spot.

code.label: Pulse.css

sections.title: What to check
sections.text:
CheckWhy
The name matches the animation propertyA typo creates no animation and no keyframe group is applied.
Stops are in the expected orderfrom/to and percentages are shown in source order.
Every stop has the properties you expectA missing declaration at one stop can produce a visible jump.
Vendor-neutral property namesThe engine uses standard CSS property names; verify transforms and filters in the styles pane.
Read-only view
The Animations tab does not scrub a timeline or pause an animation. Use it
to verify definitions, then edit the component stylesheet or the Elements
tab to change them.

sections.title: A practical workflow
sections.text:
- Locate the animation name in the left pane.
- Confirm every expected stop and property is present.
- Switch to Elements and select the animated element.
- Check the matched rule that declares animation, including duration, easing and iteration count.
- Edit the stylesheet, then reopen or refresh the inspector to see the updated keyframes.
Performance
Prefer transforms and opacity for continuous animations. The Performance
tab will show whether an animation is contributing to layout or render
spikes.

topics.title: Using the deploy tab
topics.summary:
Deploy builds the application targets into the project's
builds folder, then serves that folder over the local network
so a device or phone can download the result. The same server page accepts
screenshots and writes them into the project's debug folder.

sections.title: Build targets
sections.text:
The tab discovers the enabled hosts from the app project and lists them as
build targets. The standard entries are:
TargetOutputResult
Desktopbuilds/desktopFramework-dependent desktop build.
Androidbuilds/androidSigned APK copied from the build output.
WebAssemblybuilds/wasmStatic site with index.html at the folder root.
Build All runs the targets in order. Each row also has its
own build button. Builds run on a worker thread, so the app frame loop keeps
running while dotnet works.

sections.title: Output layout
sections.text:
MyApp/
├── builds/
│   ├── desktop/
│   ├── android/
│   │   └── MyApp-Signed.apk
│   └── wasm/
│       ├── index.html

└── debug/          # screenshots uploaded from the Deploy server page
The default build configuration is Release. The deploy
service exposes it as DevTools.Builds.Configuration; change it
before starting a build. Custom targets can be added with
DevTools.Builds.AddTarget(...).

sections.title: Building
sections.text:
- Open the inspector and select Deploy.
- Choose a target row, or press Build All.
- Watch the per-target status and the shared build log at the bottom.
- Use the produced path to inspect the artifact locally, or start the download server.
Android signing
The Android target builds an APK with the project's normal signing
configuration. The signed APK is copied into builds/android
with a device-friendly file name.

sections.title: Starting the download server
sections.text:
The server turns the builds folder into a small browsable HTTP
index. Toggle it with the download-server button in the Deploy tab. While it
is running, the tab lists:
- The loopback URL, for example http://localhost:8080/.
- One URL for each active IPv4 interface, so a phone on the same network can connect.
SettingDefaultNotes
Port8080Change while stopped; the server binds when started.
Root{project}/buildsSubfolders are browsable; files download directly.
BindingAll IPv4 interfacesWorks for localhost and LAN devices.
AuthNoneUse only on a trusted local network.
Uploading screenshots
Every page served by the download server also has an upload area. Drop
screenshots onto it, or click it to browse, and each image is saved to
{project}/debug. The application can then read those files as
local context, for example to attach a visual regression screenshot to a
bug report or an agent prompt.
- The original file name is kept; a numeric suffix is added when the name already exists.
- Only image files are accepted, up to 32 MB each. Several files can be dropped at once.
- Uploads are written by the same local server, so the page must be opened from the server URL.
- The debug folder is ignored by Git in the framework repository.

sections.title: Getting a build onto a device
sections.text:
Android
- Build the Android target.
- Start the download server.
- Open the server URL on the phone or tablet.
- Open android/ and download the signed APK.
- Install it from the browser or a file manager. The device may ask you to allow installs from the browser.
Desktop
Download the files from desktop/ to the target machine. The
desktop output is framework-dependent, so the machine needs the matching
.NET runtime.
WebAssembly
The site is under wasm/. Copy that folder to any static host
that serves the right MIME types:
The download server is for downloads, not hosting the WASM app
Its file server is intentionally minimal and does not provide the full MIME
and compression behaviour a WebAssembly app expects. Use it to fetch
builds/wasm, then serve the copied site with a proper static
server.

sections.title: Network checklist
sections.text:
- Phone and computer must be on the same network.
- Allow the application through the host firewall if the LAN URL is unreachable.
- If port 8080 is taken, stop the server, change the port, and start it again.
- The server has no authentication. Stop it when you are done.
Fast iteration
Keep the Deploy tab open while iterating. Rebuild the target, refresh the
browser listing, and download the new artifact; the output folder is reused
between builds.

topics.summary:
The Elements tab is the inspector's live DOM and style editor. It shows the
same reconciled tree the renderer is drawing, including component and text
nodes.

The tab is split into two panes. The left pane is the hierarchy; the right
pane is the style editor for the selected node.

sections.title: Walking the hierarchy
sections.text:
- Click a row to select it. The style pane updates immediately.
- Use the caret to expand or collapse a node with children.
- Hover a row to highlight the corresponding element in the app.
- Component rows show the component type and can expand into their rendered output.
- Text nodes appear as quoted, non-expandable rows.

The inspect button (the crosshair in the toolbar) lets you pick an element
directly from the app. Click the picker, then click any app element. The
inspector selects it and expands its path. Inspect mode is cleared after a

sections.text:
The right pane shows an element.style group first for the
selected element, followed by matched rules. Each group lists its
declarations; the inspector groups rules by selector and keeps the live
stylesheet order.
- Click a declaration value to edit it.
- Use the colour swatch or picker for colour values.
- Open + Add property to add a declaration to a rule or to the element style.
- Edits are queued and applied on the frame thread, so the UI stays responsive.
- Element-style edits affect only the selected element; rule edits update the stylesheet.
Use element.style for experiments
Put one-off overrides in element.style first. Once a value is
right, move it into the component's CSS rule so it survives a remount.

refreshes when the app tree changes and prunes selections or expansion
entries whose nodes have left the tree. If an element is removed, its
selection is cleared safely rather than pointing at a dead node.

topics.title: Using the performance tab
topics.summary:
The Performance tab turns the last few seconds of frame work into a small
dashboard. It is designed to show where a frame goes, not to replace a
profiler.

sections.title: What is sampled
sections.text:
The host samples while the Performance tab is visible, at most every
0.25 seconds. Each graph keeps up to 120
samples. The panel refreshes roughly once per second, so the
numbers are recent but not instantaneous.
Sampling pauses when hidden
Leave the tab open while reproducing a slow interaction. Switching away
stops the sample stream, so the graph will not contain work performed while
another tab was active.

sections.title: The summary cards
sections.text:
CardMeaning
FPSWhole frames per second derived from the latest wall-clock frame time. The small line also shows the frame time in milliseconds.
CPUProcess-wide CPU usage percentage and the current thread count. The first sample has no baseline, so it reports zero.
ManagedManaged heap bytes. The secondary line shows the process working set.
GCGen 0, gen 1 and gen 2 collection counts.

sections.title: The graphs
sections.text:
Three bar graphs show the retained history. They use fixed vertical scales
so different runs are comparable:
GraphScaleUse it to spot
Frame time33 ms full heightOverall hitches and frames that missed the display budget.
Layout time16 ms full heightLayout rebuilds caused by state, styles or viewport changes.
Render time16 ms full heightDisplay-list submission and GPU-facing work.
A tall frame bar with short layout and render bars points at work outside
the measured passes, such as waiting on the platform or another thread. A
tall layout bar points at geometry churn. A tall render bar points at
display-list or submission cost.

sections.title: Frame budgets
sections.text:
Refresh rateBudget per frame
60 Hz16.7 ms
120 Hz8.3 ms
144 Hz6.9 ms
The graph scales are diagnostic aids, not hard budgets. A 16 ms layout bar
on a 144 Hz display is already too large for a smooth frame.

sections.title: A practical workflow
sections.text:
- Open the Performance tab and leave it visible.
- Reproduce one interaction, then stop. Avoid a long sequence that mixes several causes.
- Compare the three graphs. Is the spike in layout, render, or only frame time?
- Switch to Elements and inspect the subtree involved. Check for unnecessary class changes, large text updates, or layout-affecting styles.
- Reduce the work: keep subtrees stable, key list items, memoise derived data, and avoid triggering full-tree changes for local state.
Look for repeated spikes
One tall bar is often startup or a one-off allocation. A regular pattern of
spikes is the useful signal: it maps to an interaction or animation that
runs on a timer or every frame.

sections.title: What it does not tell you
sections.text:
- It does not attribute time to a specific C# method; use a sampling profiler for that.
- It does not capture GPU timings on every driver.
- It does not sample while the tab is hidden.
- It is desktop/Android inspector tooling; use browser devtools for the WASM host.

topics.title: Video reference
topics.summary:
video is a host primitive, not an element the renderer can
paint by walking children. On desktop and Android a native player decodes
the stream off the UI thread and publishes frames as textures; layout treats
the element as replaced content and the host paints the transport controls.

sections.title: Why it is special
sections.text:
ConcernHow Donkeh handles it
DecodingUses LibVLCSharp. Initialisation, demuxing, decoding and I/O run on worker threads.
PresentationDecoded frames are copied into the window's image cache as a dynamic texture, then drawn through the normal image path. The most recent frame is reused until the next one arrives.
LayoutThe element is replaced content with a default 300 × 150 box. CSS width, height, aspect ratio and object-fit apply to the frame.
ChromeWhen controls is present, the host paints and hit-tests its own play/pause, scrubber, time and volume controls. They are not DOM elements and cannot be styled individually.
LifecycleOne player per element. Players are created asynchronously, updated when attributes change, and pruned when the element leaves the tree.
This is why video needs a typed props object and a native
dependency. A plain H("video", ...) still works because
VideoProps derives from Props, but the typed
OnReady callback is only available through it.

sections.title: Basic playback
sections.text:
Native runtime required
The managed LibVLCSharp package does not replace the native
LibVLC runtime. Install VLC or ship the matching native libraries with the
app. If LibVLC cannot be initialised, the element still lays out but no
frames or controls become available.

sections.text:
On WebAssembly the element is a native HTML video element. The
browser owns decoding, controls and the media APIs, so
OnReady, VideoPlayer and the host-painted transport
controls are desktop/Android features. Use standard attributes such as
src, controls, autoplay,

large videos on one screen; the decode threads are independent, but every
visible frame still costs an upload per update.

topics.title: WebView reference
topics.summary:
A webview embeds a real browser document in your UI. On desktop,
Chromium Embedded Framework (CEF) renders the page offscreen; Donkeh uploads each
painted frame as a texture and draws it through the same display list as every
other element. The webview therefore behaves like a replaced element — it
takes part in layout, stacking order, clipping, opacity and transforms —
instead of being a separate native window floating above the app.

sections.title: What a webview actually is
sections.text:
Unlike iframe, object and embed, which are
currently just styled placeholder boxes, webview creates a live
Chromium browser. HTML, CSS and JavaScript inside it are parsed and executed by
Chromium, not by Donkeh. Donkeh only owns the element’s box and decides where
the browser’s pixels appear on screen.
The browser does not draw into the Donkeh window directly. CEF paints into an
offscreen buffer; Donkeh converts those pixels to RGBA, copies them into a texture
held by the image cache, and emits a normal image draw at the element’s paint
position. This is the same pipeline used by video frames,
which is why the webview can sit behind or in front of other content and be
clipped or transformed by its ancestors.

sections.title: Behaviour by concern
sections.text:
ConcernHow Donkeh handles it
LayoutReplaced content with a default 300 × 150 box, the width/height attributes, or CSS. The box is the browser viewport; resizing it resizes the CEF view.
PaintingEach CEF frame becomes a texture in the shared image cache and is drawn as an ImageSpec. It obeys z-index, stacking contexts, scroll offsets, clip, opacity and transforms.
InputPointer move/press/release, wheel and key events are forwarded into the browser by the host. The webview takes focus on press; focusing another control gives it back.
ThreadingCEF paints on its own UI thread. Frames are copied into a per-element buffer there and uploaded to the GPU on Donkeh’s render thread, where the OpenGL context is current.
LifecycleOne browser per element, created on the first frame where the element has a src. Browsers are disposed when their element leaves the tree; CEF is shut down when the window closes.
PlatformDesktop only. Android has no WebView-to-GLES texture bridge, and the browser host mirrors the tree to real DOM, where a native iframe is the right tool.

element props; Src,
ClassName, styles and event handlers are the standard ones. Plain

sections.title: The src attribute
sections.text:
Src accepts three forms:
- An absolute URL such as https://example.com.
- A data: URI for self-contained HTML.
- A local path, which is resolved to a file: URI so bundled or downloaded pages can be loaded.
An element without a usable src is skipped. Changing src
disposes the existing browser and creates a new one, so the page follows the prop.

sections.title: Sizing and layout
sections.text:
The default box is 300 × 150 CSS pixels, matching iframe. Use the
width and height attributes or CSS to change it. The
element’s border box becomes the browser viewport in device pixels; Donkeh
resizes the CEF view whenever layout changes, including when a scroll container
moves the element on screen.
Scrolling inside the loaded page is handled by Chromium. Wheel events over
the element are forwarded to the browser instead of scrolling Donkeh ancestors, so
the page scrolls naturally. Content outside the element is clipped by normal CSS
overflow rules. object-fit is not used: the frame always
fills the box.

OnReady receives a WebView object. It is a thin,
engine-independent control surface, so application code never has to reference
CefSharp directly.

do nothing.

events that land inside the element are forwarded to the browser, so they normally

document from src is ready. A single element can override it with the
loading-page attribute. OnWebViewReady is a global hook
invoked for every webview alongside the element-level OnReady prop.

Each webview owns a tab collection. Only the active tab is painted,

sections.title: Plugins and script injection
sections.text:
Plugins are the Electron-like extension point. A plugin contributes preload
scripts, registers .NET objects for JavaScript, and handles IPC messages.
Register plugins globally in WebViewOptions.Configuring, or use
view.Plugins / tab.Plugins to add and remove them for
a single view at runtime.
Scripts run at DocumentStart (as soon as the frame's V8 context
exists, before page scripts), DocumentEnd, or never
(Manual). They can be filtered by URL and restricted to the main
frame. By default each snippet is wrapped in an IIFE so it does not leak
declarations into the page; set Isolate = false to inject raw source.

The injected bridge exposes window.donkeh.send(channel, payload),
invoke(channel, payload) (a promise resolved by
message.Reply(...)), on(channel, callback) and
off(channel, callback). Set EnablePluginBridge = false
or BridgeGlobalName in WebViewOptions to replace or
rename it. Messages are JSON; use WebViewMessage.Read<T>() to
deserialize them.
Object binding uses CefSharp's legacy binding, so objects must be
registered before the browser is created. Global registrations and
plugin OnAttached hooks happen automatically at that point;
objects added later with RegisterObject bind through an
explicit CefSharp.BindObjectAsync call.

sections.title: Input and focus in detail
sections.text:
Because the browser is offscreen, the operating system delivers input to the
Donkeh window, not to Chromium. Donkeh translates and forwards it:
- Mouse move, press and release are converted to browser-local CSS pixels and sent with the current modifier state.
- Wheel deltas are forwarded so the page scrolls instead of an ancestor container.
- Key down, key up and character events are forwarded while a webview has focus.
- Pressing inside a webview focuses it and blurs any previous webview; focusing another Donkeh control returns focus.
This means keyboard shortcuts and text input go to the page while it is focused.
It also means the browser’s native chrome is unavailable: there is no address
bar, context menu integration or IME composition window. Your app owns navigation
through the WebView controller.

sections.title: Performance
sections.text:
This implementation uses CEF’s CPU offscreen rendering path. Each painted
frame is copied from BGRA to RGBA and uploaded in full with
glTexSubImage2D; dirty rectangles are not used yet. Cost therefore
scales with the element’s pixel area and with how often the page repaints.
Keep webviews to sensible sizes, and prefer static pages for large surfaces.
The accelerated shared-texture path exists in CEF but is intentionally not used
here. Swapping it in later would change only how frames are produced — the
element, layout, input and paint integration would stay the same.

sections.title: Current limitations
sections.text:
- Desktop hosts only; Android and the browser DOM host do not create a CEF browser.
- Popup widgets painted by Chromium (for example native select dropdowns and context menus) are not composited into the Donkeh frame.
- Load state, title and history flags are available on WebViewTab; full CEF request/navigation events are not bridged into Donkeh events yet.
- IME composition ranges and drag-and-drop from the page are not wired.
- Every frame is uploaded in full; there is no dirty-region upload.
- The native CEF runtime must be shipped with the application output.
